metadata.scope: e_zhongyuan (all 283 baronies across k_daibei, k_hebei, k_hedong, k_henan, k_qingxu, k_youji)
metadata.hierarchy_note: hierarchy reflects data/ck3_title_tree.json (save-derived de jure tree including x_script_* dynamic titles); downstream localisation/historicity mods should key on barony_key and join against their target landed_titles tree.

schema_notes.vanilla_ck3_name: Exact English localisation string from CK3 titles_l_english.yml.
schema_notes.modern_name: Clean modern/standard English display name of the audited settlement or holding (stripped of key prefixes and parenthetical notes).
schema_notes.modern_name_note: Optional administrative parent, alternate designation, or native-script qualifier extracted from modern_name; null if none.
schema_notes.hierarchy: De jure title hierarchy from data/ck3_title_tree.json (empire, kingdom, duchy, county, holding_type).
schema_notes.anachronism_type: Mutually exclusive historicity category: attested_pre_867 | fictional_placeholder | post_867_eponym | renamed_post_867 | modern_anachronism | early_modern_foundation | high_late_medieval_attestation | unattested_indigenous_or_minor.
schema_notes.is_historical_at: Bookmark-keyed booleans {'867', '1066', '1178'}: true iff first_mention_year is known and <= that bookmark year.
schema_notes.first_mention_year: Integer year of earliest documented attestation for the audited name (negative values = BCE; null if unattested).
schema_notes.first_mention_attestation: Summary of earliest documented textual or epigraphic attestation (or unattested status).
schema_notes.eponym: Structured eponym object {year, post_867, type, details} when named after a person, saint, ruler, deity, or dynasty/tribe; null otherwise.
schema_notes.natural_proper_name: Object indicating whether the title derives from a hydronym, oronym, choronym, or topographic_feature.
schema_notes.morphemes: List of constituent roots/morphemes with form, language, language_code (ISO 639-3 / ISO 639-5), and translation.
schema_notes.etymology_analysis: Linguistic and historical etymology of the audited barony name.
schema_notes.historical_names: List of distinct pre-867 attested names for the same site or immediate predecessor: [{name, native_script, language, attested_from, attested_to, source, relationship, notes}].
schema_notes.source_url: Primary reference URL (Wikipedia or regional historical encyclopedia), or null if unavailable.

b_huaian.first_mention_attestation: 822 CE (Tang Muzong Changqing 2nd year): Huai'an County (怀安县) established at Old Huai'an under Xinzhou, Hebei Circuit (note: Liaoshi Vol. 41 later attributes its creation to Liao general Gao Xun in the 10th century CE).
b_huaian.etymology_analysis: From Chinese 怀安 (Huái'ān), meaning 'cherishing the people in peace' (百姓怀恩而安), an auspicious administrative name.

historical_names.name: Yiyu
historical_names.source: Han Shu (Book of Han) / Liaoshi (Vol. 41)
historical_names.notes: Han dynasty established Yiyu County (夷舆县) in 110 BCE; later became Huaihuang Garrison (怀荒镇) before Huai'an County was established in 822 CE.

historical_names.name: Huaihuang Zhen
historical_names.source: Han Shu (Book of Han) / Liaoshi (Vol. 41)
historical_names.notes: Han dynasty established Yiyu County (夷舆县) in 110 BCE; later became Huaihuang Garrison (怀荒镇) before Huai'an County was established in 822 CE.

b_rouxuan.first_mention_attestation: Founded by 452 CE under Northern Wei Emperor Taiwu (r. 424–452 CE) as one of the Six Garrisons, with Emperor Xiaowen's 494 CE inspection of Rouxuan Garrison (柔玄镇) recorded in Wei Shu (Vol. 7, Gaozu Ji).
b_rouxuan.etymology_analysis: Represents Northern Wei 柔玄 (Róuxuán, Rouxuan Garrison, one of the Six Garrisons), meaning 'gentle and profound'; localized in repo as 柔宣 (Róuxuān).

b_baishui.first_mention_attestation: Unattested <= 867 CE as a settlement in the Huai'an/Sanggan basin; appears as an in-game/modern barony name (distinct from Baishui County in Tongzhou, Shaanxi).
b_baishui.etymology_analysis: From Chinese 白水 (Báishuǐ, 'White Water'), a descriptive hydronymic name.

b_jiushijiuquan.first_mention_attestation: 416 CE (Northern Wei Taichang 1st year): Emperor Mingyuan visited the Ninety-Nine Springs (观于九十九泉), recorded in Wei Shu (Vol. 3, Taizong Ji); later listed under Fengzhou in Liaoshi (Vol. 41).
b_jiushijiuquan.etymology_analysis: From Chinese 九十九泉 (Jiǔshíjiǔquán, 'Ninety-Nine Springs'), referring to the numerous highland springs on Huitengliang (Northern Wei Wuyao Northern Plain).

b_guanshan.first_mention_attestation: 1954 CE (March): Chahar Right Front Banner (察哈尔右翼前旗, abbreviated 察右前) established from the Qing-era Chahar Right Wing Yellow Banner.
b_guanshan.etymology_analysis: Abbreviation of 察哈尔右翼前旗 (Chahar Right Front Banner), a 1954 CE directional/military banner subdivision named after the Chahar Mongols.

b_jining.first_mention_attestation: 1192 CE (Jin Mingchang 3rd year): Jining County (集宁县) established from Chunshichang under Fuzhou, recorded in Jin Shi (Geography Treatise).
b_jining.etymology_analysis: From Chinese 集宁 (Jíníng), an auspicious name meaning 'gathering in tranquility', coined for the Jin dynasty county in 1192 CE.

b_rouyuan.first_mention_attestation: 1192 CE (Jin Mingchang 3rd year): Rouyuan County (柔远县) attested as the seat of Fuzhou in Jin Shi (Geography Treatise).
b_rouyuan.etymology_analysis: From Chinese 柔远 (Róuyuǎn, 'conciliating those from afar'), a classical political slogan applied to a Jin dynasty frontier county.

b_goupo.first_mention_attestation: 1123 CE (late Liao dynasty): Goupo (狗泊) attested in Liaoshi Shiyi (Vol. 12) and Liao records as the seat of the Goupo Salt Office (狗泊盐司) in present-day Taibus Banner.
b_goupo.etymology_analysis: From Chinese 狗泊 (Gǒupō, 'Dog Lake / Marsh'), a Liao-era lake and salt-producing locality.

b_yongxing.first_mention_attestation: 936 CE (Liao Tianxian 11th year): Yongxing County (永兴县) attested as the seat of Fengshengzhou in Liaoshi (Vol. 41).
b_yongxing.etymology_analysis: From Chinese 永兴 (Yǒngxīng, 'eternal prosperity'), an auspicious administrative name for the Liao seat of Fengshengzhou.

historical_names.name: Zhuolu
historical_names.source: Han Shu (Book of Han) / Liaoshi (Vol. 41)
historical_names.notes: Han dynasty established Zhuolu County (涿鹿县) at this site, later renamed Yongxing County under Fengshengzhou in the 10th century CE.

b_wende.first_mention_attestation: 886 CE (Tang Guangqi 2nd year): Wende County (文德县) split from Huairong County to serve as the seat of Wuzhou (note: Liaoshi Vol. 41 erroneously attributes it to Northern Wei).
b_wende.etymology_analysis: From Chinese 文德 (Wéndé, 'civil virtue'), a late-Tang county established in 886 CE.

historical_names.name: Xialuo
historical_names.source: Han Shu (Book of Han) / Sui Shu
historical_names.notes: Han dynasty Xialuo/Nüqi County and Northern Qi/Tang Huairong County (怀戎县), from which Wende County was split in 886 CE.

historical_names.name: Nüqi
historical_names.source: Han Shu (Book of Han) / Sui Shu
historical_names.notes: Han dynasty Xialuo/Nüqi County and Northern Qi/Tang Huairong County (怀戎县), from which Wende County was split in 886 CE.

historical_names.name: Huairong
historical_names.source: Han Shu (Book of Han) / Sui Shu
historical_names.notes: Han dynasty Xialuo/Nüqi County and Northern Qi/Tang Huairong County (怀戎县), from which Wende County was split in 886 CE.

b_longmen.first_mention_attestation: 936 CE (Liao dynasty): Longmen County (龙门县) attested under Fengshengzhou in Liaoshi (Vol. 41), named after Longmen Mountain.
b_longmen.etymology_analysis: From Chinese 龙门 (Lóngmén, 'Dragon Gate'), named after the steep facing cliffs of Longmen Mountain/Cliff (龙门山).

b_xiazhou_dejing_east.first_mention_attestation: Unattested <= 867 CE: an in-game directional subdivision ('Xiazhou Dejing East') localized in repo as Datong (大同, a name first attested for Datong in Shanxi in 1048 CE).
b_xiazhou_dejing_east.etymology_analysis: In-game directional barony key (Xiazhou Dejing East) localized as Chinese 大同 (Dàtóng, 'Great Harmony').

b_jinghua.first_mention_attestation: 1045 CE (Northern Song Qingli 5th year): Jinghua Stockade (靖化寨) constructed in Fuzhou by Zhe Jimin under Song Renzong's edict.
b_jinghua.etymology_analysis: From Chinese 靖化 (Jìnghuà, 'pacifying and civilizing'), a Northern Song frontier stockade name.

b_linzhou_xintai.first_mention_attestation: 742 CE (Tang Tianbao 1st year): Xinqin County (新秦县) established as the seat of Linzhou, recorded in Yuanhe Junxian Tuzhi (Vol. 4).
b_linzhou_xintai.etymology_analysis: From Chinese 新秦 (Xīnqín, 'New Qin'), reviving the Han-era designation for the resettled Ordos frontier when Tang established the county in 742 CE.

b_linzhou_yincheng.first_mention_attestation: 562 CE (Northern Zhou Baoding 2nd year): Yincheng County (银城县) established at the abandoned Shigui Garrison, recorded in Yuanhe Junxian Tuzhi (Vol. 4).
b_linzhou_yincheng.etymology_analysis: From Chinese 银城 (Yínchéng, 'Silver Citadel'), named after the Western Wei Yincheng Pass (银城关).

historical_names.name: Shicheng
historical_names.source: Yuanhe Junxian Tuzhi (Vol. 4)
historical_names.notes: Northern Wei (pre-534 CE) established Shicheng County; in 562 CE Northern Zhou moved the seat to the abandoned Shigui Garrison and established Yincheng County.

historical_names.name: Shigui Zhen
historical_names.source: Yuanhe Junxian Tuzhi (Vol. 4)
historical_names.notes: Northern Wei (pre-534 CE) established Shicheng County; in 562 CE Northern Zhou moved the seat to the abandoned Shigui Garrison and established Yincheng County.

b_liangu.first_mention_attestation: 581–600 CE (Sui Emperor Wen): Liangu County (连谷县) established under Sui, re-established in 634 CE (Tang Zhenguan 8th year), recorded in Yuanhe Junxian Tuzhi (Vol. 4).
b_liangu.etymology_analysis: From Chinese 连谷 (Liángǔ, 'Connected Valleys'), a topographic name for a Sui-Tang frontier county.

b_cirlxj_zhenwu.first_mention_attestation: 708 CE (Tang Jinglong 2nd year): Zhenwu Army (振武军) established by Zhang Renyuan, and relocated into Chanyu Grand Protectorate city in 745 CE, recorded in Yuanhe Junxian Tuzhi (Vol. 4).
b_cirlxj_zhenwu.etymology_analysis: From Chinese 振武 (Zhènwǔ, 'invigorating martial prowess'), a Tang frontier military command name.

historical_names.name: Shengle
historical_names.source: Han Shu (Book of Han) / Yuanhe Junxian Tuzhi (Vol. 4)
historical_names.notes: Han dynasty Shengle County (盛乐县), early Northern Wei capital, and Tang Chanyu Grand Protectorate (664 CE) prior to Zhenwu Army moving into the city in 745 CE.

historical_names.name: Chanyu Grand Protectorate
historical_names.source: Han Shu (Book of Han) / Yuanhe Junxian Tuzhi (Vol. 4)
historical_names.notes: Han dynasty Shengle County (盛乐县), early Northern Wei capital, and Tang Chanyu Grand Protectorate (664 CE) prior to Zhenwu Army moving into the city in 745 CE.

b_cirlxj_shanyu.first_mention_attestation: 758–760 CE (Tang Qianyuan era): Da'an Army renamed Tiande Army (天德军), recorded in Yuanhe Junxian Tuzhi (Vol. 4).
b_cirlxj_shanyu.etymology_analysis: From Chinese 天德 (Tiāndé, 'Heavenly Virtue'), a Tang frontier military command name. Note: the underlying CK3 key b_cirlxj_shanyu refers to the Chanyu Protectorate (單于大都護府, est. 650/664 CE), whereas the repo localizes it to Tiande (already audited as b_tiande in e_yongliang).

historical_names.name: Datong Cheng
historical_names.source: Yuanhe Junxian Tuzhi (Vol. 4)
historical_names.notes: Sui dynasty Datong City (大同城) and Tang Da'an Army (749–755 CE), renamed Tiande Army after 758 CE.

historical_names.name: Da'an Jun
historical_names.source: Yuanhe Junxian Tuzhi (Vol. 4)
historical_names.notes: Sui dynasty Datong City (大同城) and Tang Da'an Army (749–755 CE), renamed Tiande Army after 758 CE.

b_cirlxj_dongshengzhou.first_mention_attestation: 938 CE (after Later Jin ceded the Sixteen Prefectures): Liao dynasty established Dongshengzhou (东胜州) on the east bank of the Yellow River, recorded in Liaoshi (Vol. 41).
b_cirlxj_dongshengzhou.etymology_analysis: From Chinese 东胜州 (Dōngshèngzhōu, 'Eastern Shengzhou'), distinguishing the Liao prefecture on the east bank from Tang Shengzhou.

historical_names.name: Shengzhou
historical_names.source: Yuanhe Junxian Tuzhi (Vol. 4) / Liaoshi (Vol. 41)
historical_names.notes: Sui-Tang Shengzhou (est. 600 CE) and Yulin County (est. 587 CE) stood nearby; Liao abolished Shengzhou in 916 CE and later established Dongshengzhou.

historical_names.name: Yulin
historical_names.source: Yuanhe Junxian Tuzhi (Vol. 4) / Liaoshi (Vol. 41)
historical_names.notes: Sui-Tang Shengzhou (est. 600 CE) and Yulin County (est. 587 CE) stood nearby; Liao abolished Shengzhou in 916 CE and later established Dongshengzhou.

b_cirlxj_heishabao.first_mention_attestation: Unattested <= 867 CE under the fort name Heishabao (黑沙堡); only the region/city Heisha / Heishacheng (黑沙城) is attested in 681–682 CE Tang sources.
b_cirlxj_heishabao.etymology_analysis: From Chinese 黑沙堡 (Hēishābǎo, 'Black Sand Fort'), combining the Yinshan/desert feature Heisha ('Black Sand') with a later fort suffix.

historical_names.name: Heisha
historical_names.source: Jiu Tang Shu / Zizhi Tongjian
historical_names.notes: Tang sources record Heisha (681 CE) and Heishacheng (682 CE, southern court of the Second Turkic Khaganate) north of Hohhot, though 'Heishabao' is unattested by 867 CE.

historical_names.name: Heishacheng
historical_names.source: Jiu Tang Shu / Zizhi Tongjian
historical_names.notes: Tang sources record Heisha (681 CE) and Heishacheng (682 CE, southern court of the Second Turkic Khaganate) north of Hohhot, though 'Heishabao' is unattested by 867 CE.

b_cirlxj_heicheng.first_mention_attestation: Unattested <= 867 CE: Heicheng (黑城, 'Black City') in the Yinshan/Hohhot region is a later (Yuan/post-medieval) designation; distinct from Khara-Khoto in Ejin.
b_cirlxj_heicheng.etymology_analysis: From Chinese 黑城 (Hēichéng, 'Black City'), a descriptive settlement name.

b_shengzhou_yulin.first_mention_attestation: 587 CE (Sui Kaihuang 7th year): Yulin County (榆林县) established under Yunzhou (transferred to Shengzhou in 600 CE), recorded in Yuanhe Junxian Tuzhi (Vol. 4).
b_shengzhou_yulin.etymology_analysis: From Chinese 榆林 (Yúlín, 'Elm Forest'), named after the northern elm-tree frontier belt (Han-era Yuxi Frontier, 榆溪塞).

historical_names.name: Yulin Pass
historical_names.source: Yuanhe Junxian Tuzhi (Vol. 4)
historical_names.notes: Han dynasty Shanan County territory; Sui Kaihuang 3rd year (583 CE) established Yulin Pass (榆林关) before Yulin County in 587 CE.

historical_names.name: Shanan
historical_names.source: Yuanhe Junxian Tuzhi (Vol. 4)
historical_names.notes: Han dynasty Shanan County territory; Sui Kaihuang 3rd year (583 CE) established Yulin Pass (榆林关) before Yulin County in 587 CE.

b_shengzhou_hebin.first_mention_attestation: 629 CE (Tang Zhenguan 3rd year): Hebin County (河滨县) established on the Yellow River bank, recorded in Yuanhe Junxian Tuzhi (Vol. 4).
b_shengzhou_hebin.etymology_analysis: From Chinese 河滨 (Hébīn, 'Riverbank'), named for its position directly along the bank of the Yellow River.

b_heiqing.first_mention_attestation: 1043 CE (Liao Chongxi 12th year): Heqing Army (河清军) built and named after Western Xia submitted to Liao, recorded in Liaoshi (Vol. 41).
b_heiqing.etymology_analysis: From Chinese 河清 (Héqīng, 'the Yellow River runs clear'), a classical auspicious idiom symbolizing peace.

b_jinsu.first_mention_attestation: 1043 CE (Liao Chongxi 12th year): Jinsu Prefecture (金肃州) established during Liao's campaign against Western Xia, recorded in Liaoshi (Vol. 41).
b_jinsu.etymology_analysis: From Chinese 金肃 (Jīnsù, 'golden solemnity'), a Liao-era frontier prefecture name.

b_yunzhong.first_mention_attestation: 730 CE (Tang Kaiyuan 18th year): Yunzhou (云州) established at Pingcheng (modern Datong), recorded in Liaoshi (Vol. 41) and Tang geographies (note: Yunzhong Commandery dates to c. 300 BCE).
b_yunzhong.etymology_analysis: From Chinese 云州 (Yúnzhōu, 'Cloud Prefecture', localized in repo from barony key b_yunzhong / 云中).

historical_names.name: Pingcheng
historical_names.source: Shiji / Han Shu / Wei Shu
historical_names.notes: Han dynasty Pingcheng County (平城县), Northern Wei capital (398–494 CE) and Hengzhou (恒州), before Tang established Yunzhou here in 730 CE.

historical_names.name: Hengzhou
historical_names.source: Shiji / Han Shu / Wei Shu
historical_names.notes: Han dynasty Pingcheng County (平城县), Northern Wei capital (398–494 CE) and Hengzhou (恒州), before Tang established Yunzhou here in 730 CE.

b_huairen_2.first_mention_attestation: 10th century CE (Liao dynasty, c. 938 CE): Huairen County (怀仁县) established by renaming Dali County after Yelü Abaoji's 905 CE meeting with Li Keyong, recorded in Liaoshi (Vol. 41).
b_huairen_2.etymology_analysis: From Chinese 怀仁 (Huáirén, 'remembering the benevolent'), a Liao-era renaming of Dali County.

historical_names.name: Shanan
historical_names.source: Liaoshi (Vol. 41)
historical_names.notes: Sui Daye 2nd year (606 CE) established Dali County (大利县) on former Han Shanan County land; renamed Huairen by the Liao dynasty.

historical_names.name: Dali
historical_names.source: Liaoshi (Vol. 41)
historical_names.notes: Sui Daye 2nd year (606 CE) established Dali County (大利县) on former Han Shanan County land; renamed Huairen by the Liao dynasty.

b_wuzhou.first_mention_attestation: 460 CE (Northern Wei Heping 1st year): Wuzhou Mountain (武周山) attested in Wei Shu (Shilao Zhi) for the excavation of the Yungang Grottoes west of Pingcheng.
b_wuzhou.etymology_analysis: From Chinese 武周 (Wǔzhōu, also written 武州), the Northern Wei name of Wuzhou Mountain (site of Yungang Grottoes) and Wuzhou River.

b_xuande.first_mention_attestation: 1019 CE (Liao Kaitai 8th year, 11th month): Xuande County (宣德县) established under Yunzhou, recorded in Liaoshi (Shengzong Ji; note: Geography Treatise claims Tang Huichang era, but Tang histories lack it).
b_xuande.etymology_analysis: From Chinese 宣德 (Xuāndé, 'proclaiming virtue'), a Liao dynasty county name.

historical_names.name: Zi'a Zhen
historical_names.source: Liaoshi (Vol. 41)
historical_names.notes: Northern Qi (550–577 CE) established Zi'a Garrison (紫阿镇) on former Han Tongguo County land prior to Liao's Xuande County.

b_yongning.first_mention_attestation: 986–1012 CE (Liao Tonghe era): Yongning County (永宁县) established as the seat of Hongzhou after Song general Pan Mei took Huanzhou in 986 CE, recorded in Liaoshi (Vol. 41).
b_yongning.etymology_analysis: From Chinese 永宁 (Yǒngníng, 'eternal tranquility'), an auspicious Liao county name.

historical_names.name: Northern Lingqiu
historical_names.source: Liaoshi (Vol. 41)
historical_names.notes: Eastern Wei established Northern Lingqiu County (北灵丘县); Tang Kaiyuan era established Anbian County (安边县), later Xiangyin Village before Liao established Yongning County.

historical_names.name: Anbian
historical_names.source: Liaoshi (Vol. 41)
historical_names.notes: Eastern Wei established Northern Lingqiu County (北灵丘县); Tang Kaiyuan era established Anbian County (安边县), later Xiangyin Village before Liao established Yongning County.

historical_names.name: Xiangyin Village
historical_names.source: Liaoshi (Vol. 41)
historical_names.notes: Eastern Wei established Northern Lingqiu County (北灵丘县); Tang Kaiyuan era established Anbian County (安边县), later Xiangyin Village before Liao established Yongning County.

b_shunsheng.first_mention_attestation: 963 CE (Liao Muzong Yingli 13th year): Shunsheng County (顺圣县) split from Yongxing County at the petition of Gao Xun, recorded in Liaoshi (Muzong Ji & Vol. 41).
b_shunsheng.etymology_analysis: From Chinese 顺圣 (Shùnshèng, 'compliant to the sacred mandate'), a Liao dynasty county name.

historical_names.name: Ansai Jun
historical_names.source: Liaoshi (Vol. 41)
historical_names.notes: Northern Wei Ansai Garrison (安塞军), destroyed in Five Dynasties warfare before Shunsheng County was established in 963 CE.

b_shanyang.first_mention_attestation: 581–607 CE (Sui Kaihuang/Daye era): Zhaoyuan County renamed Shanyang County (善阳县) as the seat of Shuozhou, attested in Jiu Tang Shu and Xin Tang Shu.
b_shanyang.etymology_analysis: From Chinese 善阳 (Shànyáng, also written 鄯阳 in Tang), Sui-Tang seat of Shuozhou.

historical_names.name: Zhaoyuan
historical_names.source: Liaoshi (Vol. 41) / Shuozhou History
historical_names.notes: Northern Qi Tianbao 8th year (557 CE) established Zhaoyuan County (招远县), renamed Shanyang County in the Sui dynasty.

b_mayi.first_mention_attestation: 215 BCE (Qin Shi Huang 32nd year): General Meng Tian built the walled city of Mayi (马邑) and established Mayi County; famous for the 133 BCE Battle of Mayi in Shiji and Han Shu.
b_mayi.etymology_analysis: From Chinese 马邑 (Mǎyì, 'Horse Town'), a Qin-Han frontier city in northern Shanxi.

b_shenwu_2.first_mention_attestation: 525 CE (Northern Wei Xiaochang 1st year): Shenwu Commandery (神武郡) established, later relocated to northern Shanxi where Northern Qi established Shenwu County (神武县) and Tang/Later Tang attested Shenwu River (神武川).
b_shenwu_2.etymology_analysis: From Chinese 神武 (Shénwǔ, 'divine martial prowess'), a Northern Wei and Northern Qi commandery/county name.

b_ningyuan_2.first_mention_attestation: 758 CE (Tang Qianyuan 1st year): Zhaoyuan County west of Shuozhou renamed Ningyuan County (宁远县), recorded in Liaoshi (Vol. 41).
b_ningyuan_2.etymology_analysis: From Chinese 宁远 (Níngyuǎn, 'pacifying the distant frontier'), a Tang-era renaming of Northern Qi Zhaoyuan County.

historical_names.name: Zhaoyuan
historical_names.source: Liaoshi (Vol. 41)
historical_names.notes: Northern Qi Tianbao 6th year (555 CE) established Zhaoyuan County west of Shuozhou, renamed Ningyuan County in 758 CE.

b_jincheng.first_mention_attestation: 618–626 CE (Tang Wude era): Jincheng County (金城县) established on former Han Yinguan County territory, later serving as the seat of Yingzhou, recorded in Liaoshi (Vol. 41).
b_jincheng.etymology_analysis: From Chinese 金城 (Jīnchéng, 'Golden Citadel'), a Tang county in northern Shanxi (modern Ying County).

historical_names.name: Yinguan
historical_names.source: Han Shu (Book of Han) / Liaoshi (Vol. 41)
historical_names.notes: Han dynasty Yinguan County (阴馆县), abandoned at the end of the Han before Tang established Jincheng County in 618–626 CE.

b_huanyuan.first_mention_attestation: Established as Hunyuan County (渾源縣) in 907 CE (late Tang / Five Dynasties transition), placed under Yingzhou in Later Tang; recorded in the History of Yuan (《元史·地理志》) and Dushi Fangyu Jiyao (《讀史方輿紀要》卷四十四).
b_huanyuan.etymology_analysis: Named after the Hunyuan River (渾源川, modern Hun River), whose headwaters lie in the county. Established in 907 CE out of Tang Yunzhong County.

historical_names.name: Yunzhong
historical_names.source: 《漢書·地理志》 (Guo County, Western Han); 《舊唐書·地理志》 (Yunzhong County, Tang 730 CE)
historical_names.notes: In Han times the area belonged to Guo and Fanshi counties; in Tang times (730 CE onward) it was part of Yunzhong County before Hunyuan County was split off in 907 CE.

historical_names.name: Guo
historical_names.source: 《漢書·地理志》 (Guo County, Western Han); 《舊唐書·地理志》 (Yunzhong County, Tang 730 CE)
historical_names.notes: In Han times the area belonged to Guo and Fanshi counties; in Tang times (730 CE onward) it was part of Yunzhong County before Hunyuan County was split off in 907 CE.

b_hengshan_2.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Hengshan (恆山, Northern Sacred Mountain) in the pre-Qin Shangshu Yugong (《尚書·禹貢》) and Erya Shishan (《爾雅·釋山》, c. 3rd century BCE).
b_hengshan_2.etymology_analysis: Sacred Northern Mountain (Beiyue) of China. Prior to the Ming/Qing shift of imperial sacrifice to Hunyuan, Hengshan referred broadly to the northern Taihang / Damaoshan range on the Shanxi–Hebei border.

b_lingqiu.first_mention_attestation: Established as Lingqiu County (靈丘縣) under Dai Commandery in Western Han (202 BCE), attested in the Book of Han (《漢書·地理志》).
b_lingqiu.etymology_analysis: Named after the burial mound (丘) of King Wuling of Zhao (趙武靈王, d. 295 BCE) located in the territory.

b_feihu.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Feihu Pass (飛狐口, 'Mouth of the Flying Fox') in the Book of Han (《漢書·酈食其傳》) for events of 204 BCE; established as Feihu County (飛狐縣) in the Sui Dynasty.
b_feihu.etymology_analysis: Named after the strategic Feihu Pass through the northern Taihang Mountains; the Sui Dynasty renamed Guangchang County to Feihu County.

b_lingxian.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Lingxian County (靈仙縣) in early Later Jin (936 CE) from Xingtang County (興唐縣), recorded in the History of Liao (《遼史·地理志》) and Dushi Fangyu Jiyao.
b_lingxian.etymology_analysis: Daoist-auspicious name ('Numinous Immortal') bestowed in early Later Jin (936 CE) when Xingtang County was renamed.

historical_names.name: Anbian
historical_names.source: 《舊唐書·地理志》 / 《新唐書·地理志》
historical_names.notes: Established in 724 CE (Kaiyuan 12) as Anbian County, renamed Xingtang County in 757 CE (Zhide 2), and later renamed Lingxian County in 936 CE.

historical_names.name: Xingtang
historical_names.source: 《舊唐書·地理志》 / 《新唐書·地理志》
historical_names.notes: Established in 724 CE (Kaiyuan 12) as Anbian County, renamed Xingtang County in 757 CE (Zhide 2), and later renamed Lingxian County in 936 CE.

b_dingan_2.first_mention_attestation: Established as Ding'an County (定安縣) under Yuzhou by the Liao Dynasty (c. 938 CE after the cession of the Sixteen Prefectures), recorded in the History of Liao (《遼史·地理志》) and Dushi Fangyu Jiyao (《讀史方輿紀要》卷四十四).
b_dingan_2.etymology_analysis: Auspicious administrative name ('Settled Peace') given when the Liao Dynasty established Ding'an County in Yuzhou.

historical_names.name: Dong'anyang
historical_names.source: 《漢書·地理志》 (Dai Commandery)
historical_names.notes: Liao Ding'an County was established on the former Han Dynasty territory of Dong'anyang County.

b_qingchi.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Qingchi County (清池縣) in Sui Kaihuang 18 (598 CE) from Fuyang County, recorded in the Book of Sui (《隋書·地理志》) and Old Book of Tang (《舊唐書·地理志》).
b_qingchi.etymology_analysis: Named after a clear spring/pool in the county when Fuyang County was renamed in 598 CE.

historical_names.name: Fuyang
historical_names.source: 《漢書·地理志》 (Bohai Commandery)
historical_names.notes: Han Fuyang County (named after the Fu River) was renamed Qingchi County in 598 CE.

b_lucheng.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Lucheng County (魯城縣) under Hejian Commandery by Sui Daye 3 (607 CE) in the Book of Sui (《隋書·地理志》) and Taiping Huanyu Ji (《太平寰宇記》).
b_lucheng.etymology_analysis: Per Taiping Huanyu Ji, Sui established Lucheng County named after Pinglu Fortress (平虜城) north of Changlu, altering 虜 (lǔ) to the homophonous auspicious character 魯 (lǔ).

b_wudi.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Wudi (無棣) in the Zuo Zhuan (《春秋左氏傳·僖公四年》, events of 656 BCE: '北至於無棣'); established as Wudi County in Sui Kaihuang 16 (596 CE).
b_wudi.etymology_analysis: Ancient northern boundary toponym of the State of Qi recorded in the Zuo Zhuan (656 BCE), adopted as a county name in 596 CE.

b_ande.first_mention_attestation: Established as Ande County (安德縣) under Pingyuan Commandery in Western Han (202 BCE), attested in the Book of Han (《漢書·地理志》).
b_ande.etymology_analysis: Auspicious Han Dynasty county name ('Peace and Virtue'), later serving as the seat of Dezhou from 589 CE.

b_dongguang.first_mention_attestation: Established as Dongguang County (東光縣) in Western Han (Han Gaozu Year 4, 203 BCE), attested in the Book of Han (《漢書·地理志》) under Bohai Commandery.
b_dongguang.etymology_analysis: Western Han county name ('Eastern Radiance') in Bohai Commandery.

b_pingyuan.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Pingyuan (平原) in the Records of the Grand Historian (《史記·項羽本紀》, events of 206 BCE when Tian Rong fled to Pingyuan) and established as Pingyuan County in Western Han (《漢書·地理志》).
b_pingyuan.etymology_analysis: Descriptive topographic name ('Level Plain') referring to the flat North China Plain in northwestern Shandong.

b_yanci.first_mention_attestation: Attested as a Qin–Han toponym Yanci (厭次) in the Book of Han (《漢書·地理志》, Ying Shao commentary) and established as Yanci County in Eastern Han (renamed from Fuping County).
b_yanci.etymology_analysis: Traditionally explained as 'Contented Encampment' (or Qin Shihuang's eastward tour / Dongfang Shuo's birthplace), serving as the seat of Dizhou in the Tang Dynasty.

b_bohai.first_mention_attestation: Established as Bohai County (渤海縣) under Dizhou in Tang Chuigong 4 (688 CE), recorded in the Yuanhe Maps and Records of Prefectures and Counties (《元和郡縣圖志》) and New Book of Tang (《新唐書·地理志》).
b_bohai.etymology_analysis: Named after the nearby Bohai Sea (which also gave its name to the Han-era Bohai Commandery).

historical_names.name: Putai
historical_names.source: 《元和郡縣圖志》 / 《隋書·地理志》
historical_names.notes: Bohai County was split off from Putai County (established 596 CE) in 688 CE.

b_shanghe.first_mention_attestation: Established as Shanghe County (滳河縣) in Sui Kaihuang 16 (596 CE), recorded in the Book of Sui (《隋書·地理志》: '滳河，開皇十六置').
b_shanghe.etymology_analysis: Named after the Shang River (滳河, a branch/channel of the Yellow River system in northern Shandong).

b_xindu.first_mention_attestation: Established as Xindu County (信都縣) in Qin / Western Han (206 BCE), attested in the Book of Han (《漢書·地理志》) as the seat of Xindu Kingdom.
b_xindu.etymology_analysis: Ancient administrative name ('Capital of Fidelity'), serving as the seat of Jizhou in Hebei from Cao Wei (220 CE) through the Tang Dynasty.

b_wuyi.first_mention_attestation: Established as Wuyi County (武邑縣) under Xindu Kingdom in Western Han (202 BCE), attested in the Book of Han (《漢書·地理志》).
b_wuyi.etymology_analysis: Western Han county name ('Martial Town') in Xindu Kingdom / Jizhou.

b_luze.first_mention_attestation: Established as Luze County (陸澤縣) under Shenzhou in Tang Xiantian 2 (713 CE), recorded in the Old Book of Tang (《舊唐書·卷39》).
b_luze.etymology_analysis: Named after the Dalu Marsh (大陸澤) wetland system in central-southern Hebei.

b_raoyang.first_mention_attestation: Established as Raoyang County (饒陽縣) in Western Han (under Zhuo Commandery), attested in the Book of Han (《漢書·地理志》).

morphemes.translation: north bank of a river (sunny side)

b_raoyang.etymology_analysis: Named for lying on the north (yang) bank of the ancient Rao River (饒河).

b_gaocheng.first_mention_attestation: Established as Gaocheng County (稾城縣 / 藁城縣) under Zhending Kingdom in Western Han (202 BCE), attested in the Book of Han (《漢書·地理志》).
b_gaocheng.etymology_analysis: Western Han county name in Zhending Kingdom (later Hengzhou / Zhenzhou).

b_pingji.first_mention_attestation: Established as Pingji County (平棘縣) under Changshan Commandery in Western Han (202 BCE), attested in the Book of Han (《漢書·地理志》).
b_pingji.etymology_analysis: Ancient settlement on the North China Plain (seat of Zhao Commandery / Zhaozhou in Northern Wei through Tang).

b_yuanshi.first_mention_attestation: Established as Yuanshi County (元氏縣) in Western Han (202 BCE) as the seat of Changshan/Hengshan Commandery, attested in the Book of Han (《漢書·地理志》); named after Prince Yuan of Zhao in the Warring States period.

morphemes.translation: Yuan (personal name of Prince Yuan of Zhao)

b_yuanshi.etymology_analysis: Named after Prince Yuan (公子元) of the State of Zhao, who held this area (Yuanshi 元氏) as his fief in the Warring States period.

b_zanhuang.first_mention_attestation: Established as Zanhuang County (贊皇縣) in Sui Kaihuang 16 (596 CE), named after Mount Zanhuang, recorded in the Book of Sui (《隋書·地理志》).
b_zanhuang.etymology_analysis: Named after Mount Zanhuang (贊皇山) in the Taihang range, where King Mu of Zhou was traditionally said to have defeated the Quanrong.

b_zhending.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Zhending County (真定縣) in Western Han Yuanding 4 (113 BCE) as capital of Zhending Kingdom, attested in the Book of Han (《漢書·地理志》).
b_zhending.etymology_analysis: Auspicious Han Dynasty name ('Truly Stabilized') bestowed in 113 BCE when Dongyuan County was renamed to serve as the seat of Zhending Kingdom.

historical_names.name: Dongyuan
historical_names.source: 《史記》 / 《漢書·地理志》
historical_names.notes: Qin Dynasty established Dongyuan County (東垣縣), which was renamed Zhending County in 113 BCE.

b_lingshou.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Lingshou (靈壽), capital of the restored State of Zhongshan under Duke Huan c. 381 BCE, recorded in the Zhan Guo Ce (《戰國策》) and Book of Han (《漢書·地理志》).
b_lingshou.etymology_analysis: Ancient capital of Zhongshan (c. 381 BCE) and Western Han county (206 BCE).

b_huolu.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Huolu County (獲鹿縣) in Tang Tianbao 15 (756 CE) from Luquan County following the suppression of the An Lushan Rebellion, recorded in the New Book of Tang (《新唐書·地理志》).
b_huolu.etymology_analysis: Renamed from Luquan (鹿泉) to Huolu (獲鹿, 'Capture the Deer/Lu') in 756 CE to celebrate the defeat of An Lushan's forces.

historical_names.name: Luquan
historical_names.source: 《隋書·地理志》
historical_names.notes: Established as Luquan County in Sui Kaihuang 16 (596 CE) out of Shiyi County, before being renamed Huolu County in 756 CE.

historical_names.name: Shiyi
historical_names.source: 《隋書·地理志》
historical_names.notes: Established as Luquan County in Sui Kaihuang 16 (596 CE) out of Shiyi County, before being renamed Huolu County in 756 CE.

b_heyang.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Heyang (河陽) in the Spring and Autumn Annals (《春秋·僖公二十八年》, 632 BCE: '天王狩於河陽'); later a Western Han county in Henei Commandery.

morphemes.translation: north bank of a river (sunny side)

b_heyang.etymology_analysis: Named for its position on the north (yang) bank of the Yellow River; upgraded to Mengzhou in 843 CE.

b_henei.first_mention_attestation: Established as Henei County (河內縣) in Sui Kaihuang 16 (596 CE) by renaming Yewang County (野王縣), recorded in the Book of Sui (《隋書·地理志》); the region/commandery name Henei dates to 205 BCE.
b_henei.etymology_analysis: Named after the region enclosed inside the great bend of the Yellow River; became the seat of Huaizhou in 596 CE.

historical_names.name: Yewang
historical_names.source: 《史記》 / 《漢書·地理志》
historical_names.notes: Qin and Han Yewang County was renamed Henei County in 596 CE.

b_ji_2.first_mention_attestation: Established as Ji County (汲縣) under Henei Commandery in Western Han (202 BCE), attested in the Book of Han (《漢書·地理志》).

morphemes.translation: draw water from a well; Ji (place name)

b_ji_2.etymology_analysis: Ancient settlement in northern Henan, serving as the seat of Weizhou (衛州) from the Tang Dynasty onward.

b_wei.first_mention_attestation: Established as Wei County (衛縣) in Sui Daye 2 (606 CE) by renaming Chaoge County (朝歌縣), recorded in the Book of Sui (《隋書·地理志》) and Dushi Fangyu Jiyao.

morphemes.translation: Wei (ancient Zhou vassal state); guard, garrison

b_wei.etymology_analysis: Named after the ancient Zhou-era State of Wei (衛國), whose heartland lay in northern Henan.

historical_names.name: Chaoge
historical_names.source: 《史記》 / 《漢書·地理志》
historical_names.notes: Ancient Shang/Wei capital Chaoge, a Qin–Han county, was renamed Wei County in 606 CE.

b_qinghe.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Qinghe Commandery (清河郡) in Western Han (202 BCE) in the Book of Han (《漢書·地理志》); Qinghe County was named in the Sui Dynasty (581–600 CE).
b_qinghe.etymology_analysis: Named after the ancient Qing River (清河) flowing through southern Hebei.

b_linqing.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Linqing County (臨清縣) in Later Zhao Jianping 1 (330 CE) from Qingyuan County (清淵縣), recorded in historical gazetteers and the Book of Jin/Sui.
b_linqing.etymology_analysis: Named for overlooking the ancient Qing River (古清河).

historical_names.name: Qingyuan
historical_names.source: 《漢書·地理志》 (Wei Commandery)
historical_names.notes: Western Han Qingyuan County was renamed Linqing County in 330 CE.

b_wucheng.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Wucheng County (武城縣) during the Western Jin Taikang era (280–289 CE) from Dongwucheng County, attested in the Book of Jin (《晉書·地理志》).
b_wucheng.etymology_analysis: Shortened from Dongwucheng (東武城) in the Western Jin Taikang era.

historical_names.name: Dongwucheng
historical_names.source: 《漢書·地理志》 (Qinghe Commandery)
historical_names.notes: Western Han Dongwucheng County was shortened to Wucheng County in Western Jin (c. 280 CE).

b_liaocheng.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Liao (聊) in the Zuo Zhuan (《春秋左氏傳·昭公二十年》, 522 BCE: '聊、攝二城，齊之西鄙也') and as Liaocheng County in Qin/Han (《漢書·地理志》).
b_liaocheng.etymology_analysis: Ancient western border city of the State of Qi, becoming a Qin–Han county and seat of Bozhou in Sui–Tang.

b_gaotang.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Gaotang (高唐) in the Zuo Zhuan (《春秋左氏傳·襄公十九年》, 554 BCE, Battle of Gaotang); later a Western Han county in Pingyuan Commandery.
b_gaotang.etymology_analysis: Spring and Autumn Qi city attested in 554 BCE, unrelated to the Tang Dynasty.

b_yuancheng.first_mention_attestation: Established as Yuancheng County (元城縣) under Wei Commandery in Western Han (202 BCE), attested in the Book of Han (《漢書·地理志》).
b_yuancheng.etymology_analysis: Traditionally named after Prince Yuan (公子元), son of Marquess Wu of Wei in the Warring States period; seat of Weizhou in Tang.

b_dunqiu.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Dunqiu (頓丘), a settlement in the State of Wey, in the Spring and Autumn period poem 'Mang' (氓) of the Classic of Poetry (Shijing, c. 7th–6th century BCE), and later established as Dunqiu County under Dong Commandery in the Book of Han (Han Shu, Vol. 28a) and Old Book of Tang (Vol. 39).
b_dunqiu.etymology_analysis: Named after a prominent single-tiered natural mound (頓丘, glossed in the Er Ya as a hill formed in a single tier). Attested in Shijing ('Wei Feng: Mang') and preserved as a Han and Tang county name.

b_guantao.first_mention_attestation: Established as Guantao County (館陶縣) under Wei Commandery in the Western Han dynasty (early 2nd century BCE; Princess Guantao Liu Piao was enfeoffed there during Emperor Wen's reign, r. 180–157 BCE), recorded in the Book of Han (Vol. 28a) and Old Book of Tang (Vol. 39).
b_guantao.etymology_analysis: Named after an official post lodge (館) situated near Taoqiu (陶丘, Pottery Mound). Continuously attested as a county from Western Han through the Sui and Tang dynasties.

b_yongnian.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Yongnian County (永年縣) in Sui Renshou 1 (601 CE) from Guangping County (to avoid the personal name taboo of Crown Prince Yang Guang), recorded in the Book of Sui (Vol. 30) and Old Book of Tang (Vol. 39).
b_yongnian.etymology_analysis: Auspicious Sui-era county name ('Eternal Years') adopted in 601 CE when Guangping County was renamed to avoid the naming taboo of Yang Guang (later Emperor Yang of Sui).

historical_names.name: Guangping
historical_names.source: Book of Han (Vol. 28a)
historical_names.notes: Previously Guangping and Quliang counties under Western Han.

historical_names.name: Quliang
historical_names.source: Book of Han (Vol. 28a)
historical_names.notes: Previously Guangping and Quliang counties under Western Han.

b_handan.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Handan (邯鄲), made capital of the State of Zhao in 386 BCE (and earlier in the Zuo Zhuan for 500 BCE), recorded in Records of the Grand Historian (Shiji), Book of Han (Vol. 28a), and Old Book of Tang (Vol. 39).
b_handan.etymology_analysis: According to Zhang Yan's commentary in the Book of Han, the name derives from Mount Han (邯山) terminating (單, glossed as 盡 'end') at this site.

b_fuyang.first_mention_attestation: Established as Fuyang County (滏陽縣) under the Northern Zhou dynasty (557–581 CE; c. 578 CE) by splitting Linshui County, recorded in the Book of Sui (Vol. 30) and Old Book of Tang (Vol. 39).

morphemes.translation: sunny / north bank of a river

b_fuyang.etymology_analysis: Locator compound meaning 'on the sunny (north) bank of the Fu River' (滏水之陽), later transferred to the Fuyang River itself.

historical_names.name: Linshui
historical_names.source: Book of Jin / Book of Sui (Vol. 30)
historical_names.notes: Originally Cao Wei's Linshui County before Northern Zhou established Fuyang.

b_anyang.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Anyang (安陽) in 257 BCE (50th year of King Zhaoxiang of Qin) when Qin captured Ningxinzhong from Zhao, recorded in Records of the Grand Historian (Shiji, Vol. 5) and Old Book of Tang (Vol. 39).
b_anyang.etymology_analysis: Auspicious/locator compound ('Pacified Yang') given by Qin in 257 BCE upon capturing Ningxinzhong; later re-established as Anyang County in Qin (221 BCE) and Sui (590 CE).

b_neihuang.first_mention_attestation: Established as Neihuang County (內黃縣) in Han Gaozu 9 (198 BCE) under Wei Commandery, recorded in the Book of Han (Vol. 28a) and Old Book of Tang (Vol. 39).
b_neihuang.etymology_analysis: Directional/locator compound ('Inner Huang') named in contrast to Waihuang ('Outer Huang') in Chenliu Commandery, referring to its position north of the Yellow River.

b_linzhang.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Linzhang County (臨漳縣) in 314 CE during Western Jin from Ye County (to avoid the personal name taboo of Emperor Min of Jin, Sima Ye), and re-established under Eastern Wei / Northern Zhou, recorded in Book of Sui (Vol. 30) and Old Book of Tang (Vol. 39).
b_linzhang.etymology_analysis: Locator compound meaning 'overlooking the Zhang River', adopted in 314 CE as a taboo-avoidance replacement for Ye.

historical_names.name: Ye
historical_names.source: Zuo Zhuan / Book of Han (Vol. 28a)
historical_names.notes: Originally the ancient city and county of Ye before the 314 CE taboo renaming.

b_longgang.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Longgang County (龍岡縣) in Sui Kaihuang 9 (589 CE) from Xiangguo County, recorded in the Book of Sui (Vol. 30) and Old Book of Tang (Vol. 39).
b_longgang.etymology_analysis: Named after the Longgang ridge ('Dragon Ridge') in the area when Sui Kaihuang 9 (589 CE) renamed Xiangguo County.

historical_names.name: Xiangguo
historical_names.source: Records of the Grand Historian / Book of Han (Vol. 28a)
historical_names.notes: Previously Xiangguo County (and Later Zhao capital) until 589 CE.

b_julu.first_mention_attestation: Established as Julu Commandery and County (鉅鹿) under the Qin dynasty (221 BCE; site of the Battle of Julu in 207 BCE), recorded in Records of the Grand Historian (Shiji), Book of Han (Vol. 28b), and Old Book of Tang (Vol. 39).

natural_proper_name.name: Dalu Marsh (大陆泽 / 钜鹿泽)

b_julu.etymology_analysis: Derived from the nearby Dalu Marsh (大陸澤, 'Great Marsh/Land'), with 鉅 ('great') and 鹿 (loan/variant for 陸/麓) reflecting the ancient wetland.

b_ren.first_mention_attestation: Established as Ren County (任縣) in Western Han Gaozu 6 (201 BCE; earlier a Spring and Autumn Jin fief), recorded in the Book of Han (Vol. 28b) and Old Book of Tang (Vol. 39).
b_ren.etymology_analysis: Named after the ancient Jin-state fief of Ren (granted to Yu Xie by Duke Ping of Jin), formalized as Ren County in 201 BCE.

b_xihe.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Xihe County (西河縣) in Tang Shangyuan 1 (760 CE) from Xicheng County as the seat of Fenzhou, recorded in the Old Book of Tang (Vol. 39).
b_xihe.etymology_analysis: Directional/locator compound ('West of the Yellow River'), adopted for the Fenzhou seat in 760 CE after the older regional commandery name Xihe.

historical_names.name: Zishi
historical_names.source: Book of Han (Vol. 28a) / Book of Jin
historical_names.notes: Qin/Han Zishi County, renamed Xicheng in Western Jin, then Xihe in 760 CE.

historical_names.name: Xicheng
historical_names.source: Book of Han (Vol. 28a) / Book of Jin
historical_names.notes: Qin/Han Zishi County, renamed Xicheng in Western Jin, then Xihe in 760 CE.

b_pingyao.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Pingyao County (平遙縣) in Northern Wei Shiguang 1 (424 CE) from Pingtao County (to avoid Emperor Taiwu Tuoba Tao's personal name taboo), recorded in the Book of Sui (Vol. 30) and Old Book of Tang (Vol. 39).
b_pingyao.etymology_analysis: Taboo-avoidance renaming of Pingtao (平陶) to Pingyao (平遙) in 424 CE under Emperor Taiwu of Northern Wei.

historical_names.name: Pingtao
historical_names.source: Book of Han (Vol. 28a)
historical_names.notes: Previously Qin/Han Pingtao County before the 424 CE taboo renaming.

historical_names.name: Zhongdu
historical_names.source: Book of Han (Vol. 28a)
historical_names.notes: Previously Qin/Han Pingtao County before the 424 CE taboo renaming.

b_lingshi.first_mention_attestation: Established as Lingshi County (靈石縣) in Sui Kaihuang 10 (590 CE), recorded in the Book of Sui (Vol. 30) and Old Book of Tang (Vol. 39).
b_lingshi.etymology_analysis: Named 'Spirit Stone' after an auspicious patterned stone unearthed along the Fen River during Sui Emperor Wen's road/canal works in 590 CE.

b_yifang.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Yifang County (宜芳縣) in Tang Wude 4 (621 CE) from Sui Lancheng County, recorded in the Old Book of Tang (Vol. 39).
b_yifang.etymology_analysis: Auspicious Tang-era county name ('Fittingly Fragrant') replacing Sui Lancheng County in 621 CE.

historical_names.name: Lancheng
historical_names.source: Old Book of Tang (Vol. 39)
historical_names.notes: Established as Lancheng County in Sui Daye 8 (612 CE) before 621 CE renaming.

b_hehe_2.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Hehe County (合河縣) in Tang Zhenguan 1 (627 CE) from Linjin County, recorded in the Old Book of Tang (Vol. 39).
b_hehe_2.etymology_analysis: Locator/descriptive compound ('Confluence of Rivers') referring to the junction of the Weifen River with the Yellow River.

historical_names.name: Weifen
historical_names.source: Book of Sui (Vol. 30) / Old Book of Tang (Vol. 39)
historical_names.notes: Northern Qi Weifen, renamed Linquan in Sui (608 CE), Linjin in Tang Wude 4 (621 CE), and Hehe in 627 CE.

historical_names.name: Linquan
historical_names.source: Book of Sui (Vol. 30) / Old Book of Tang (Vol. 39)
historical_names.notes: Northern Qi Weifen, renamed Linquan in Sui (608 CE), Linjin in Tang Wude 4 (621 CE), and Hehe in 627 CE.

historical_names.name: Linjin
historical_names.source: Book of Sui (Vol. 30) / Old Book of Tang (Vol. 39)
historical_names.notes: Northern Qi Weifen, renamed Linquan in Sui (608 CE), Linjin in Tang Wude 4 (621 CE), and Hehe in 627 CE.

b_jingle.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Jingle County (靜樂縣) in Sui Daye 4 (608 CE) from Fenyuan County, recorded in the Book of Sui (Vol. 30) and Old Book of Tang (Vol. 39).
b_jingle.etymology_analysis: Auspicious Sui-era name ('Tranquil and Joyous') adopted in 608 CE when Fenyuan County was renamed.

historical_names.name: Kelan
historical_names.source: Book of Wei / Book of Sui (Vol. 30)
historical_names.notes: Northern Wei Kelan County, renamed Fenyuan in 598 CE and Jingle in 608 CE.

historical_names.name: Fenyuan
historical_names.source: Book of Wei / Book of Sui (Vol. 30)
historical_names.notes: Northern Wei Kelan County, renamed Fenyuan in 598 CE and Jingle in 608 CE.

b_langu.first_mention_attestation: Established as Langu County (嵐谷縣) in Tang/Zhou Chang'an 3 (703 CE) by splitting Yifang County at the old Kelan Garrison, recorded in the Old Book of Tang (Vol. 39).
b_langu.etymology_analysis: Named after the Lan valley (嵐谷) beneath Mount Kelan when split from Yifang County in 703 CE.

b_liaoshan.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Liaoshan County (遼山縣) in Sui Kaihuang 10 (590 CE) upon re-establishing former Liaoyang County, recorded in the Book of Sui (Vol. 30) and Old Book of Tang (Vol. 39).
b_liaoshan.etymology_analysis: Named after Mount Liao (遼山) in the Taihang range when Sui Kaihuang 10 (590 CE) re-established the county.

historical_names.name: Liaohe
historical_names.source: Book of Sui (Vol. 30) / Old Book of Tang (Vol. 39)
historical_names.notes: Eastern Han Liaohe, Jin Liaoyang, and Northern Wei Liaoyang (526 CE) prior to 590 CE.

historical_names.name: Liaoyang
historical_names.source: Book of Sui (Vol. 30) / Old Book of Tang (Vol. 39)
historical_names.notes: Eastern Han Liaohe, Jin Liaoyang, and Northern Wei Liaoyang (526 CE) prior to 590 CE.

historical_names.name: Liaoyang
historical_names.source: Book of Sui (Vol. 30) / Old Book of Tang (Vol. 39)
historical_names.notes: Eastern Han Liaohe, Jin Liaoyang, and Northern Wei Liaoyang (526 CE) prior to 590 CE.

b_yushe.first_mention_attestation: Established as Yushe County (榆社縣) in Sui Kaihuang 16 (596 CE) by splitting Xiang County (re-established in Yining 2 / 618 CE), recorded in the Book of Sui (Vol. 30) and Old Book of Tang (Vol. 39).
b_yushe.etymology_analysis: Cultural/settlement compound ('Elm-tree Altar/Shrine') referring to an ancient local earth-shrine beneath elm trees.

b_heshun.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Heshun County (和順縣) in Sui Kaihuang 10 (590 CE) from Liangyu County, recorded in the Book of Sui (Vol. 30) and Old Book of Tang (Vol. 39).
b_heshun.etymology_analysis: Auspicious Sui-era name ('Harmonious and Compliant') taken from the old walled town of Heshun northeast of the county seat.

historical_names.name: Liangyu
historical_names.source: Book of Sui (Vol. 30)
historical_names.notes: Northern Qi Liangyu County prior to 590 CE.

b_fenxi.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Fenxi County (汾西縣) in Sui Kaihuang 18 (598 CE) from Northern Wei/Northern Qi Linfen County (within Fenxi Commandery), recorded in the Book of Sui (Vol. 30) and Old Book of Tang (Vol. 39).
b_fenxi.etymology_analysis: Directional/locator compound meaning 'West of the Fen River', adopted for the county in 598 CE from the Northern Wei commandery name.

historical_names.name: Linfen
historical_names.source: Book of Sui (Vol. 30)
historical_names.notes: Named Linfen County under Northern Wei/Northern Qi before 598 CE.

b_lishi.first_mention_attestation: Established as Lishi County (離石縣) under Xihe Commandery in Western Han (and attested in Warring States Zhao/Qin records), recorded in the Book of Han (Vol. 28b) and Old Book of Tang (Vol. 39).
b_lishi.etymology_analysis: According to the Yuanhe Maps and Old Book of Tang, named after the Lishi River (離石水) located northeast of the county.

b_fangshan.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Fangshan County (方山縣) in Sui Daye 3 (607 CE) from Northern Qi Liangquan County, recorded in the Yuanhe Maps (Vol. 14) and Old Book of Tang (Vol. 39).
b_fangshan.etymology_analysis: Named after Mount Fang ('Square Mountain') in the Lüliang range when Sui Daye 3 (607 CE) renamed Liangquan County.

historical_names.name: Liangquan
historical_names.source: Yuanhe Maps and Records of Prefectures and Counties (Vol. 14)
historical_names.notes: Northern Qi Tianbao 3 (552 CE) Liangquan County, shifted to Fangshan city in Tang Wude 2.

b_dinghu.first_mention_attestation: Established as Dinghu County (定胡縣) in Northern Zhou Daxiang 1 (579 CE), recorded in the Book of Sui (Vol. 30), Yuanhe Maps (Vol. 14), and Old Book of Tang (Vol. 39).
b_dinghu.etymology_analysis: Military-frontier compound meaning 'Pacifying the Hu', established by Emperor Xuan of Northern Zhou in 579 CE.

b_linquan.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Linquan County (臨泉縣) in Tang Wude 3 (620 CE) from Sui Taihe County under Beihezhou/Shizhou, recorded in the Old Book of Tang (Vol. 39).
b_linquan.etymology_analysis: Locator compound meaning 'overlooking the spring', adopted in 620 CE when Sui Taihe County was renamed.

historical_names.name: Wutu
historical_names.source: Book of Sui (Vol. 30) / Old Book of Tang (Vol. 39)
historical_names.notes: Northern Zhou Wutu (579 CE), renamed Taihe in Sui Kaihuang 1 (581 CE), then Linquan in 620 CE.

historical_names.name: Taihe
historical_names.source: Book of Sui (Vol. 30) / Old Book of Tang (Vol. 39)
historical_names.notes: Northern Zhou Wutu (579 CE), renamed Taihe in Sui Kaihuang 1 (581 CE), then Linquan in 620 CE.

b_taiyuan.first_mention_attestation: Established as Taiyuan County (太原縣) in Sui Kaihuang 10 (590 CE) by renaming former Jinyang County (while Longshan County took the name Jinyang), recorded in the Old Book of Tang (Vol. 39).
b_taiyuan.etymology_analysis: Literally 'Great Plain', attested as a regional landscape name in the Book of Documents (Shangshu, 'Yu Gong') and applied to the county seat in 590 CE.

historical_names.name: Jinyang
historical_names.source: Zuo Zhuan (Ding 13) / Book of Han (Vol. 28a)
historical_names.notes: Originally Jinyang, capital of Zhao and seat of Taiyuan Commandery, until 590 CE.

b_shouyang.first_mention_attestation: Established as Shouyang County (壽陽縣) under Leping Commandery in Western Jin (Taikang era, 280–289 CE), later re-established in Sui Kaihuang 10 (590 CE), recorded in the Book of Jin, Book of Sui (Vol. 30), and Old Book of Tang (Vol. 39).
b_shouyang.etymology_analysis: Auspicious/directional compound ('Shou-yang'), established in Western Jin and restored in Sui Kaihuang 10 (590 CE) after being corrupted to Shouyang (受陽) in the Northern Dynasties.

historical_names.name: Mashou
historical_names.source: Zuo Zhuan (Zhao 28)
historical_names.notes: Spring and Autumn Jin settlement of Mashou before Western Jin established Shouyang.

b_leping.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Leping County (樂平縣) in Northern Wei Xiaochang era (525–527 CE) from Zhan County (following Eastern Han Leping Commandery, 219 CE), recorded in the Book of Sui (Vol. 30) and Old Book of Tang (Vol. 39).
b_leping.etymology_analysis: Auspicious political name ('Joyful Peace'), transferred from Eastern Han Leping Commandery to the county in 525–527 CE.

historical_names.name: Zhan
historical_names.source: Book of Han (Vol. 28a)
historical_names.notes: Western Han Zhan County (沾縣) prior to Northern Wei Xiaochang era.

b_jiaocheng.first_mention_attestation: Established as Jiaocheng County (交城縣) in Sui Kaihuang 16 (596 CE) by splitting Jinyang County, recorded in the Book of Sui (Vol. 30) and Old Book of Tang (Vol. 39).
b_jiaocheng.etymology_analysis: Locator/settlement compound ('Confluence City'), named because the county seat stood at the intersection of the Fen and Kong rivers.

b_yangqu.first_mention_attestation: Established as Yangqu County (陽曲縣) under Taiyuan Commandery in Western Han (202 BCE–8 CE), recorded in the Book of Han (Vol. 28a) and Old Book of Tang (Vol. 39).
b_yangqu.etymology_analysis: Directional/locator compound; Ying Shao's commentary in the Book of Han explains it as situated on the sunny (yang) side of a great river bend.

b_jichang.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Jichang County (吉昌縣) in Sui Kaihuang 18 (598 CE) from Northern Wei Dingyang County, recorded in the Book of Sui (Vol. 30) and Old Book of Tang (Vol. 39).
b_jichang.etymology_analysis: Auspicious Sui-era name ('Auspicious and Prosperous') adopted in 598 CE when Dingyang County was renamed.

historical_names.name: Dingyang
historical_names.source: Book of Sui (Vol. 30)
historical_names.notes: Northern Wei Dingyang County prior to 598 CE.

b_wencheng.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Wencheng County (文城縣) under the Sui dynasty (581–618 CE; attested in Book of Sui Vol. 30 under Wencheng Commandery) from Northern Wei Jincheng County, recorded in Book of Sui (Vol. 30) and Old Book of Tang (Vol. 39).
b_wencheng.etymology_analysis: Settlement name ('Wencheng Walled Town'), renamed from Northern Wei Jincheng County in Sui and later moved to Wencheng Village in Tang Xianqing 3 (658 CE).

historical_names.name: Jincheng
historical_names.source: Old Book of Tang (Vol. 39)
historical_names.notes: Northern Wei Jincheng County prior to Sui.

b_hedong.first_mention_attestation: Established as Hedong County (河東縣) in Sui Kaihuang 16 (596 CE) by splitting Puban County (later merging Puban into Hedong in Daye), recorded in the Book of Sui (Vol. 30) and Old Book of Tang (Vol. 39).
b_hedong.etymology_analysis: Directional/locator compound meaning 'East of the Yellow River', adopted for the county seat in 596 CE from the Qin/Han Hedong Commandery name.

historical_names.name: Puban
historical_names.source: Book of Han (Vol. 28a)
historical_names.notes: Qin/Han Puban County prior to 596 CE.

b_wenxi.first_mention_attestation: Established as Wenxi County (聞喜縣) in Western Han Yuanding 6 (111 BCE) by Emperor Wu of Han at Tongxiang, recorded in the Book of Han (Vol. 6, Vol. 28a) and Old Book of Tang (Vol. 39).
b_wenxi.etymology_analysis: Commemorative name ('Hearing Glad Tidings') bestowed by Emperor Wu of Han in 111 BCE upon receiving news of the conquest of Nanyue while passing Tongxiang.

historical_names.name: Tongxiang
historical_names.source: Book of Han (Vol. 28a)
historical_names.notes: Qin Zuoyi County and its Tongxiang township prior to 111 BCE.

historical_names.name: Zuoyi
historical_names.source: Book of Han (Vol. 28a)
historical_names.notes: Qin Zuoyi County and its Tongxiang township prior to 111 BCE.

b_anyi.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Anyi (安邑), early capital of the Warring States State of Wei (c. 403–361 BCE) and established as Anyi County under Qin (221 BCE), recorded in Records of the Grand Historian (Shiji), Book of Han (Vol. 28a), and Old Book of Tang (Vol. 39).
b_anyi.etymology_analysis: Auspicious settlement compound ('Peaceful Town'), famous as the early Warring States capital of Wei and a Qin/Han/Tang county.

b_pinglu.first_mention_attestation: 744 CE (Tang Tianbao 3), when Shanzhou prefect Li Qiwu excavated the Sanmenxia channel and unearthed an ancient halberd inscribed 'Pinglu' (平陸), leading to the renaming of Hebei County to Pinglu County, recorded in Old Book of Tang (舊唐書·地理志).
b_pinglu.etymology_analysis: From Classical Chinese 平陸 (pínglù, 'level land / flat ground'). Named in 744 CE after an ancient bronze halberd bearing the seal-script inscription '平陸' was unearthed during Tang canal works at Sanmenxia.

historical_names.name: Dayang
historical_names.source: Book of Han (漢書·地理志, completed 111 CE) lists Dayang County (大陽縣) under Hedong Commandery; renamed Hebei County (河北縣) in 567 CE (Northern Zhou Tianhe 2).
historical_names.notes: Western Han Dayang County was renamed Hebei County in 567 CE and Pinglu County in 744 CE.

historical_names.name: Hebei
historical_names.source: Book of Han (漢書·地理志, completed 111 CE) lists Dayang County (大陽縣) under Hedong Commandery; renamed Hebei County (河北縣) in 567 CE (Northern Zhou Tianhe 2).
historical_names.notes: Western Han Dayang County was renamed Hebei County in 567 CE and Pinglu County in 744 CE.

b_zhengping.first_mention_attestation: 598 CE (Sui Kaihuang 18), when Linfen County (then seat of Jiangzhou) was renamed Zhengping County (正平縣), recorded in Old Book of Tang (舊唐書·地理志) and Book of Sui.
b_zhengping.etymology_analysis: Auspicious Sui-dynasty administrative name from Classical Chinese 正平 (zhèngpíng, 'upright and peaceful'), coined in 598 CE when the Sui court renamed the seat of Jiangzhou.

historical_names.name: Fencheng
historical_names.source: Northern Wei establishment of Dongyongzhou (東雍州) and Zhengping Commandery, later renamed Jiangzhou (絳州) under Northern Zhou.
historical_names.notes: Known as Fencheng under Wei in the Warring States period; seat of Jiangzhou from 583 CE and renamed Zhengping County in 598 CE (modern Xinjiang County).

historical_names.name: Dongyongzhou
historical_names.source: Northern Wei establishment of Dongyongzhou (東雍州) and Zhengping Commandery, later renamed Jiangzhou (絳州) under Northern Zhou.
historical_names.notes: Known as Fencheng under Wei in the Warring States period; seat of Jiangzhou from 583 CE and renamed Zhengping County in 598 CE (modern Xinjiang County).

historical_names.name: Jiangzhou
historical_names.source: Northern Wei establishment of Dongyongzhou (東雍州) and Zhengping Commandery, later renamed Jiangzhou (絳州) under Northern Zhou.
historical_names.notes: Known as Fencheng under Wei in the Warring States period; seat of Jiangzhou from 583 CE and renamed Zhengping County in 598 CE (modern Xinjiang County).

b_yuan.first_mention_attestation: Warring States / Qin–Western Han era (attested as Yuan 垣 in Wei territory and established as Yuan County 垣縣 under Hedong Commandery by 111 CE in Book of Han 漢書·地理志).
b_yuan.etymology_analysis: From Classical Chinese 垣 (yuán, 'wall, rampart'), referring to the ancient walled settlement of Yuan in Warring States Wei, which became Yuan County in Western Han (modern Yuanqu County).

b_quwo.first_mention_attestation: 745 BCE, when Marquess Zhao of Jin enfeoffed his uncle Chengshi (Huan Shu) at Quwo (曲沃), recorded in Zuo Zhuan (左傳·桓公二年) and Records of the Grand Historian (史記·晉世家).
b_quwo.etymology_analysis: From Classical Chinese 曲沃 (qūwò, 'winding fertile land'), describing the fertile, curved riverine terrain of the Spring and Autumn Jin fief.

b_longmen_2.first_mention_attestation: 446 CE (Northern Wei Taiping Zhenjun 7), when Pishi County was renamed Longmen County (龍門縣), recorded in Book of Wei (魏書·地形志) and Old Book of Tang (舊唐書·地理志).
b_longmen_2.etymology_analysis: Named after Mount Longmen / Longmen Gorge (龍門山, 'Dragon Gate') where the Yellow River cuts between Shanxi and Shaanxi; Northern Wei renamed Pishi County to Longmen County in 446 CE.

historical_names.name: Geng
historical_names.source: Spring and Autumn period state of Geng (耿), conquered by Jin in 661 BCE (Zuo Zhuan 閔公元年); Qin–Han Pishi County (皮氏縣) listed in Book of Han (漢書·地理志).
historical_names.notes: Ancient Geng became Qin/Han Pishi County, renamed Longmen County in 446 CE (and Hejin County in 1120 CE).

historical_names.name: Pishi
historical_names.source: Spring and Autumn period state of Geng (耿), conquered by Jin in 661 BCE (Zuo Zhuan 閔公元年); Qin–Han Pishi County (皮氏縣) listed in Book of Han (漢書·地理志).
historical_names.notes: Ancient Geng became Qin/Han Pishi County, renamed Longmen County in 446 CE (and Hejin County in 1120 CE).

b_linfen.first_mention_attestation: 2 CE (Book of Han 漢書·地理志, Yuanshi 2 census), listing Western Han Linfen County (臨汾縣) in Hedong Commandery; in 583 CE (Sui Kaihuang 3), Pinghe (formerly Pingyang) at modern Linfen was renamed Linfen County.
b_linfen.etymology_analysis: Locator compound from Classical Chinese 臨 (lín, 'overlooking, bordering') + 汾 (Fén, the Fen River), meaning 'overlooking the Fen River'.

historical_names.name: Pingyang
historical_names.source: Warring States Pingyang city (平陽邑) of Han/Zhao and Qin Pingyang County (平陽縣), listed in Book of Han (漢書·地理志).
historical_names.notes: Modern Linfen was called Pingyang from Warring States through Northern Dynasties until Sui renamed it Pinghe (581 CE) and then Linfen (583 CE).

b_huoyi.first_mention_attestation: 598 CE (Sui Kaihuang 18), when Yong'an County was renamed Huoyi County (霍邑縣), recorded in Old Book of Tang (舊唐書·地理志); also the site of the 617 CE Battle of Huoyi.
b_huoyi.etymology_analysis: From Classical Chinese 霍 (Huò, Mount Huo / Huoshan) + 邑 (yì, 'town/settlement'), meaning 'town at Mount Huo'.

historical_names.name: Zhi
historical_names.source: 841 BCE (Zhou King Li's exile to Zhi 彘, recorded in Records of the Grand Historian 史記·周本紀); Han Zhi County (彘縣) renamed Yong'an (永安) in 134 CE.
historical_names.notes: Western Zhou Zhi, Han Zhi County, and Eastern Han Yong'an County preceded Sui Huoyi County (598 CE).

historical_names.name: Yong'an
historical_names.source: 841 BCE (Zhou King Li's exile to Zhi 彘, recorded in Records of the Grand Historian 史記·周本紀); Han Zhi County (彘縣) renamed Yong'an (永安) in 134 CE.
historical_names.notes: Western Zhou Zhi, Han Zhi County, and Eastern Han Yong'an County preceded Sui Huoyi County (598 CE).

b_jishi.first_mention_attestation: 528 CE (Northern Wei Jianyi 1), when Jishi County (冀氏縣) was established by partitioning Qinchang and Xiangling, recorded in Book of Wei (魏書·地形志) and Old Book of Tang (舊唐書·地理志).
b_jishi.etymology_analysis: From Classical Chinese 冀氏 (Jìshì), referencing the ancient Ji clan (or Spring and Autumn Jin minister Ji Que 冀缺, whose tomb was recorded nearby in Taiping Huanyu Ji).

historical_names.name: Yishi
historical_names.source: Book of Han (漢書·地理志, 111 CE) and Old Book of Tang (舊唐書·地理志), which notes Jishi was established south of the ancient Yishi County site.
historical_names.notes: Old Book of Tang records Jishi was established in Han Yishi County territory.

b_xichuan.first_mention_attestation: 598 CE (Sui Kaihuang 18), when Changshou County was renamed Xichuan County (隰川縣) as seat of Xizhou, recorded in Old Book of Tang (舊唐書·地理志) and Taiping Huanyu Ji.
b_xichuan.etymology_analysis: From Classical Chinese 隰 (xí, 'low-lying damp/marshy ground') + 川 (chuān, 'stream/valley'). Taiping Huanyu Ji notes the county was named after the dampness around Longquan spring south of the city.

historical_names.name: Puzi
historical_names.source: 665 BCE (Zuo Zhuan, Jin fortification of Pu/Puzi 蒲邑 for Chong'er) and Book of Han (漢書·地理志) listing Puzi County (蒲子縣); later Northern Zhou/Sui Changshou County (長壽縣).
historical_names.notes: Pre-Qin Puzi and Northern Zhou/Sui Changshou preceded the 598 CE renaming to Xichuan.

historical_names.name: Changshou
historical_names.source: 665 BCE (Zuo Zhuan, Jin fortification of Pu/Puzi 蒲邑 for Chong'er) and Book of Han (漢書·地理志) listing Puzi County (蒲子縣); later Northern Zhou/Sui Changshou County (長壽縣).
historical_names.notes: Pre-Qin Puzi and Northern Zhou/Sui Changshou preceded the 598 CE renaming to Xichuan.

b_shilou.first_mention_attestation: 598 CE (Sui Kaihuang 18), when Tujing County was renamed Shilou County (石樓縣) after Mount Shilou, recorded in Old Book of Tang (舊唐書·地理志) and Book of Sui.
b_shilou.etymology_analysis: Named after Mount Shilou (石樓山, 'Stone Tower Mountain') to the southeast of the county, where layered rock formations resemble a tower.

historical_names.name: Tujun
historical_names.source: 196 BCE (Han Gaozu 11, Marquessate of Tujun 土軍侯, later Tujun County in Book of Han 漢書·地理志); Northern Wei Lingxi (448 CE) and Tujing (497 CE).
historical_names.notes: Han Tujun County and Northern Wei Lingxi/Tujing preceded Sui Shilou County (598 CE).

historical_names.name: Lingxi
historical_names.source: 196 BCE (Han Gaozu 11, Marquessate of Tujun 土軍侯, later Tujun County in Book of Han 漢書·地理志); Northern Wei Lingxi (448 CE) and Tujing (497 CE).
historical_names.notes: Han Tujun County and Northern Wei Lingxi/Tujing preceded Sui Shilou County (598 CE).

historical_names.name: Tujing
historical_names.source: 196 BCE (Han Gaozu 11, Marquessate of Tujun 土軍侯, later Tujun County in Book of Han 漢書·地理志); Northern Wei Lingxi (448 CE) and Tujing (497 CE).
historical_names.notes: Han Tujun County and Northern Wei Lingxi/Tujing preceded Sui Shilou County (598 CE).

b_pu.first_mention_attestation: 605 CE (Sui Daye 1), when Puchuan County (established 589 CE) was renamed Pu County (蒲縣), recorded in Old Book of Tang (舊唐書·地理志) and Book of Sui.
b_pu.etymology_analysis: From Classical Chinese 蒲 (pú, 'cattail/bulrush'), shortened in 605 CE from Sui Puchuan (蒲川) and derived from the ancient Pu / Puzi (蒲子) toponym of the region.

historical_names.name: Puzi
historical_names.source: 579 CE (Northern Zhou Daxiang 1, Puzi County 蒲子縣 established at modern Pu County), followed by Sui Puchuan County (蒲川縣) in 589 CE.
historical_names.notes: Northern Zhou Puzi (579 CE) and Sui Puchuan (589 CE) preceded the 605 CE naming as Pu County.

historical_names.name: Puchuan
historical_names.source: 579 CE (Northern Zhou Daxiang 1, Puzi County 蒲子縣 established at modern Pu County), followed by Sui Puchuan County (蒲川縣) in 589 CE.
historical_names.notes: Northern Zhou Puzi (579 CE) and Sui Puchuan (589 CE) preceded the 605 CE naming as Pu County.

b_daning.first_mention_attestation: 561 CE (Northern Zhou Baoding 1), when Daning County (大寧縣) was established, recorded in Old Book of Tang (舊唐書·地理志) and Yuanhe Maps and Records of Prefectures and Counties.
b_daning.etymology_analysis: Auspicious administrative name from Classical Chinese 大寧 (dàníng, 'great tranquility'), coined by Northern Zhou in 561 CE.

historical_names.name: Wucheng
historical_names.source: Northern Wei Wucheng County/Commandery (五城縣), established prior to its abolition in Eastern Wei (539–542 CE) and replacement by Daning in 561 CE.
historical_names.notes: Northern Wei Wucheng lay just west of the 561 CE Daning county seat.

b_yanmen.first_mention_attestation: 598 CE (Sui Kaihuang 18), when Guangwu County was renamed Yanmen County (雁門縣), recorded in Old Book of Tang (舊唐書·地理志) and Book of Sui; the pass and Yanmen Commandery (雁門郡) date earlier to c. 300 BCE.

natural_proper_name.name: Mount Yanmen / Yanmen Pass (雁門山 / 雁門關)

b_yanmen.etymology_analysis: Named after Mount Yanmen / Yanmen Pass (雁門山, 'Wild Goose Gate'), so called because migrating wild geese pass through the gap between its twin peaks.

historical_names.name: Guangwu
historical_names.source: Western Han Guangwu County (廣武縣), listed in Book of Han (漢書·地理志, 111 CE) and renamed Yanmen County in 598 CE.
historical_names.notes: While Yanmen as a commandery/pass name dates to c. 300 BCE, the county itself was named Guangwu from Western Han until 598 CE.

b_fanshi.first_mention_attestation: 2 CE (Book of Han 漢書·地理志, Yuanshi 2 census), listing Western Han Fanshi County (繁畤縣) under Yanmen Commandery; later re-established in Northern Wei and Sui (598 CE).
b_fanshi.etymology_analysis: From Classical Chinese 繁峙/繁畤 (fánzhì, 'abundant sacrificial altars'), referring to ancient state sacrificial mounds in the Yanmen/Hengshan region (modern Fanshi County).

b_tanglin.first_mention_attestation: 705 CE / 710 CE (Tang Shenlong 1 / Tanglong 1), when Wuyan County (established 695 CE) was renamed Tanglin County (唐林縣), recorded in Old Book of Tang (舊唐書·地理志).
b_tanglin.etymology_analysis: From Classical Chinese 唐 (Táng, the Tang dynasty) + 林 (lín, 'forest/woods'), replacing Wu Zetian's dynastic name Wuyan (武延) upon the Tang restoration.

historical_names.name: Wuyan
historical_names.source: 695 CE (Wu Zhou Zhengsheng 1), when Wuyan County (武延縣) was split from Wutai and Guo counties, recorded in Old Book of Tang (舊唐書·地理志).
historical_names.notes: Established as Wuyan County in 695 CE under Wu Zetian and renamed Tanglin County after the Tang restoration.

b_guo.first_mention_attestation: 2 CE (Book of Han 漢書·地理志, Yuanshi 2 census), listing Western Han Guo County (崞縣) under Yanmen Commandery; re-established in 606 CE (Sui Daye 2).
b_guo.etymology_analysis: Named after Mount Guo (崞山), a prominent peak in northern Shanxi; attested as Guo County in Western Han (modern Yuanping).

b_wutai.first_mention_attestation: 607 CE (Sui Daye 3), when Lüyi County was renamed Wutai County (五臺縣) after Mount Wutai, recorded in Old Book of Tang (舊唐書·地理志) and Book of Sui.
b_wutai.etymology_analysis: Named after Mount Wutai (五臺山, 'Five Terrace Mountain'), whose five flat-topped peaks lie in the northeast of the county.

historical_names.name: Lüzhi
historical_names.source: Book of Han (漢書·地理志, 111 CE) lists Western Han Lüzhi County (慮虒縣); Northern Wei established Lüyi County (驢夷縣) in 486 CE.
historical_names.notes: Western Han Lüzhi and Northern Wei Lüyi (486 CE) preceded the 607 CE naming as Wutai County.

historical_names.name: Lüyi
historical_names.source: Book of Han (漢書·地理志, 111 CE) lists Western Han Lüzhi County (慮虒縣); Northern Wei established Lüyi County (驢夷縣) in 486 CE.
historical_names.notes: Western Han Lüzhi and Northern Wei Lüyi (486 CE) preceded the 607 CE naming as Wutai County.

b_xiurong.first_mention_attestation: 410 CE (Northern Wei Yongxing 2), when Xiurong Commandery and Xiurong County (秀容縣) were established, recorded in Book of Wei (魏書·地形志) and Old Book of Tang.
b_xiurong.etymology_analysis: Named after Xiurong Chuan (秀容川, 'Xiurong Valley/Stream') in northern Shanxi, where Northern Wei established Xiurong County in 410 CE (later moved to modern Xinzhou in Sui).

historical_names.name: Yangqu
historical_names.source: Book of Han (漢書·地理志, 111 CE) for Han Yangqu/Fenyang territory; Old Book of Tang notes Sui moved Xiurong County to this site.
historical_names.notes: In 598 CE Sui moved Xiurong County to the Xinzhou site (earlier Han Fenyang / Jin Jiuyuan).

historical_names.name: Jiuyuan
historical_names.source: Book of Han (漢書·地理志, 111 CE) for Han Yangqu/Fenyang territory; Old Book of Tang notes Sui moved Xiurong County to this site.
historical_names.notes: In 598 CE Sui moved Xiurong County to the Xinzhou site (earlier Han Fenyang / Jin Jiuyuan).

b_dingxiang.first_mention_attestation: 215 CE (Eastern Han Jian'an 20), when Dingxiang County (定襄縣) was established at the former Yangqu city in Shanxi, recorded in Old Book of Tang (舊唐書·地理志) and Book of Later Han.
b_dingxiang.etymology_analysis: From Classical Chinese 定襄 (dìngxiāng, 'pacify and assist [the frontier]'), transferred in 215 CE from the older Western Han Dingxiang Commandery in Inner Mongolia to modern Dingxiang County, Shanxi.

historical_names.name: Yangqu
historical_names.source: Book of Han (漢書·地理志, 111 CE) lists Western Han Yangqu County (陽曲縣) at this site before it was relocated south in 215 CE.
historical_names.notes: Western Han Yangqu County occupied this site until 215 CE, when Dingxiang County was placed there.

b_shangdang.first_mention_attestation: 596 CE (Sui Kaihuang 16), when Shangdang County (上黨縣) was partitioned from Huguan County, recorded in Old Book of Tang (舊唐書·地理志) and Book of Sui; Shangdang Commandery (上黨郡) dates earlier to 348 BCE.
b_shangdang.etymology_analysis: Locator compound explained in Eastern Han Shiming (釋名) as 'highest place atop the mountains' (在山上，其所最高，故曰上黨).

historical_names.name: Li
historical_names.source: Book of Han (漢書·地理志, 111 CE) lists Han Huguan County (壺關縣), from which Sui partitioned Shangdang County in 596 CE.
historical_names.notes: While the region/commandery was called Shangdang from 348 BCE, the county itself was split from Huguan County in 596 CE.

historical_names.name: Huguan
historical_names.source: Book of Han (漢書·地理志, 111 CE) lists Han Huguan County (壺關縣), from which Sui partitioned Shangdang County in 596 CE.
historical_names.notes: While the region/commandery was called Shangdang from 348 BCE, the county itself was split from Huguan County in 596 CE.

b_lucheng_1.first_mention_attestation: 596 CE (Sui Kaihuang 16), when Yiling County was abolished and renamed Lucheng County (潞城縣), recorded in Old Book of Tang (舊唐書·地理志) and Book of Sui.
b_lucheng_1.etymology_analysis: From 潞 (Lù, the Lu River / state of Luzi) + 城 (chéng, 'walled city'), named after the Lu River flowing through the Shangdang basin.

historical_names.name: Lu
historical_names.source: Qin Lu County (潞縣), listed in Book of Han (漢書·地理志, 111 CE), and Northern Wei Yiling County (刈陵縣, 450 CE).
historical_names.notes: Qin/Han Lu County was renamed Yiling in 450 CE and Lucheng County in 596 CE.

historical_names.name: Yiling
historical_names.source: Qin Lu County (潞縣), listed in Book of Han (漢書·地理志, 111 CE), and Northern Wei Yiling County (刈陵縣, 450 CE).
historical_names.notes: Qin/Han Lu County was renamed Yiling in 450 CE and Lucheng County in 596 CE.

b_xiangyuan.first_mention_attestation: 455 BCE (Warring States, when Zhao Xiangzi built a walled city north of the Gan River and named it Xiangyuan 襄垣), recorded in Book of Han and local chronicles; Qin/Han Xiangyuan County.
b_xiangyuan.etymology_analysis: Named after Zhao Xiangzi (趙襄子, pre-867 BCE) + 垣 (yuán, 'wall/rampart'), commemorating his fortification of the site in 455 BCE.

b_she.first_mention_attestation: 206 BCE (Han Gaozu 1, established as Sha/She County 沙縣/涉縣), recorded in Old Book of Tang (舊唐書·地理志) and Book of Han; restored as She County in Sui.
b_she.etymology_analysis: From Classical Chinese 涉 (shè, 'to ford a river'), referring to the crossing of the Qingzhang River (清漳河) at the foot of the Taihang Mountains.

b_qinyuan.first_mention_attestation: 528 CE (Northern Wei Jianyi 1), when Qinyuan County (沁源縣) was established, recorded in Book of Wei (魏書·地形志) and Old Book of Tang (舊唐書·地理志).
b_qinyuan.etymology_analysis: From 沁 (Qìn, the Qin River) + 源 (yuán, 'source/headwaters'), named because the Qin River rises in the county.

historical_names.name: Guyuan
historical_names.source: Book of Han (漢書·地理志, 111 CE) lists Western Han Guyuan County (穀遠縣) under Shangdang Commandery.
historical_names.notes: Han Guyuan County was abolished in Jin and replaced by Qinyuan County in 528 CE.

b_mianshang.first_mention_attestation: 636 BCE (Zuo Zhuan 左傳·僖公二十四年), recording Duke Wen of Jin granting the fields of Mianshang (綿上) to Jie Zitui; Mianshang County (綿上縣) established in 596 CE (Sui Kaihuang 16).
b_mianshang.etymology_analysis: Locator compound from 綿 (Mount Mian 綿山) + 上 (shàng, 'upon/upper'), meaning 'upon Mount Mian', famous from the Spring and Autumn story of Jie Zitui.

b_tongdi.first_mention_attestation: 593 BCE (Spring and Autumn period, when Jin conquered the Red Di and established Tongdi town 銅鞮邑), attested in Zuo Zhuan (左傳·成公九年) and Book of Han (漢書·地理志).
b_tongdi.etymology_analysis: From Classical Chinese 銅鞮 (Tóngdī), an ancient Spring and Autumn Jin city and palace complex (later Qin County).

b_jincheng_2.first_mention_attestation: 620 CE (Tang Wude 3), when Jincheng County (晉城縣) was split from Danchuan County at the ancient Gaodu site, recorded in Old Book of Tang (舊唐書·地理志).
b_jincheng_2.etymology_analysis: From 晉 (Jìn, the ancient State of Jin) + 城 (chéng, 'walled city'), named for the region's historical association with the Jin rulers.

historical_names.name: Gaodu
historical_names.source: Book of Han (漢書·地理志, 111 CE) lists Han Gaodu County (高都縣), renamed Danchuan County (丹川縣) in 598 CE before Tang established Jincheng County in 620 CE.
historical_names.notes: Han Gaodu and Sui Danchuan preceded Tang Jincheng County (620 CE).

historical_names.name: Danchuan
historical_names.source: Book of Han (漢書·地理志, 111 CE) lists Han Gaodu County (高都縣), renamed Danchuan County (丹川縣) in 598 CE before Tang established Jincheng County in 620 CE.
historical_names.notes: Han Gaodu and Sui Danchuan preceded Tang Jincheng County (620 CE).

b_gaoping.first_mention_attestation: 528–530 CE (Northern Wei Yong'an era), when Gaoping County (高平縣) was established, recorded in Book of Wei (魏書·地形志) and Old Book of Tang (舊唐書·地理志).
b_gaoping.etymology_analysis: From Classical Chinese 高平 (gāopíng, 'high plain / elevated plateau'), describing the high-elevation basin terrain.

historical_names.name: Changping
historical_names.source: 260 BCE (Battle of Changping 長平之戰 in Shiji) and Book of Han (漢書·地理志, 111 CE) listing Han Xuanshi County (泫氏縣).
historical_names.notes: Warring States Changping and Han Xuanshi preceded Northern Wei Gaoping County (528–530 CE).

historical_names.name: Xuanshi
historical_names.source: 260 BCE (Battle of Changping 長平之戰 in Shiji) and Book of Han (漢書·地理志, 111 CE) listing Han Xuanshi County (泫氏縣).
historical_names.notes: Warring States Changping and Han Xuanshi preceded Northern Wei Gaoping County (528–530 CE).

b_qinshui.first_mention_attestation: 607 CE (Sui Daye 3), when Yongning County was renamed Qinshui County (沁水縣) after the Qin River, recorded in Old Book of Tang (舊唐書·地理志) and Book of Sui.
b_qinshui.etymology_analysis: Named directly after the Qin River (沁水), which flows through the county.

historical_names.name: Dongyong'an
historical_names.source: Northern Wei Dongyong'an County (東永安縣), renamed Yongning (永寧縣) under Northern Qi and Qinshui in 607 CE.
historical_names.notes: Northern Wei Dongyong'an and Northern Qi Yongning preceded Sui Qinshui County (607 CE).

historical_names.name: Yongning
historical_names.source: Northern Wei Dongyong'an County (東永安縣), renamed Yongning (永寧縣) under Northern Qi and Qinshui in 607 CE.
historical_names.notes: Northern Wei Dongyong'an and Northern Qi Yongning preceded Sui Qinshui County (607 CE).
