b_kaifeng.first_mention_attestation: Western Han (reign of Emperor Jing, r. 157–141 BCE), when Qifeng (啟封) was renamed Kaifeng (開封) to avoid the emperor's personal name Liu Qi (劉啟); listed in Book of Han (漢書·地理志).
b_kaifeng.etymology_analysis: From Classical Chinese 開封 (kāifēng, 'open/expand the borders'), altered from Spring and Autumn 啟封 (qǐfēng) due to Western Han naming taboo for Emperor Jing (Liu Qi).

historical_names.name: Qifeng
historical_names.source: Spring and Autumn Zheng town Qifeng (啟封) and 361 BCE Warring States Wei capital Daliang (大梁) recorded in Bamboo Annals and Shiji.
historical_names.notes: Spring and Autumn Qifeng was renamed Kaifeng in the 2nd century BCE; nearby Daliang/Junyi was the Warring States Wei capital.

historical_names.name: Daliang
historical_names.source: Spring and Autumn Zheng town Qifeng (啟封) and 361 BCE Warring States Wei capital Daliang (大梁) recorded in Bamboo Annals and Shiji.
historical_names.notes: Spring and Autumn Qifeng was renamed Kaifeng in the 2nd century BCE; nearby Daliang/Junyi was the Warring States Wei capital.

b_fengqiu.first_mention_attestation: Western Han (under Emperor Gaozu, r. 202–195 BCE), when Fengqiu County (封丘縣) was established, recorded in Book of Han (漢書·地理志) under Chenliu Commandery.
b_fengqiu.etymology_analysis: From Classical Chinese 封丘 (fēngqiū, 'enfeoffed hill / Fengfu's mound'), associated with the ancient State of Fengfu (封父國) and Han Gaozu's enfeoffment legend.

b_yongqiu.first_mention_attestation: Qin–Western Han era (Qin Yongqiu County 雍丘縣 under Dang Commandery, also scene of 209 BCE uprising in Shiji), listed in Book of Han (漢書·地理志).
b_yongqiu.etymology_analysis: From Classical Chinese 雍丘 (Yōngqiū), the Qin–Tang name of modern Qi County (杞縣), Henan.

historical_names.name: Qi
historical_names.source: Spring and Autumn State of Qi (杞國), attested in Chunqiu/Zuo Zhuan prior to Qin's establishment of Yongqiu County.
historical_names.notes: Ancient State of Qi preceded Qin Yongqiu County (renamed back to Qi County in Later Jin / Jin dynasty).

b_chenliu.first_mention_attestation: 225 BCE (Qin Shi Huang 22, following the conquest of Wei, when Chenliu County 陳留縣 was established), also recorded in Shiji (史記·酈生陸賈列傳) and Book of Han (漢書·地理志).
b_chenliu.etymology_analysis: From 陳 (State of Chen) + 留 (Liu), explained by Meng Kang in Book of Han commentary as 'Liu, formerly a town of Zheng, later annexed by Chen, hence called Chenliu.'

historical_names.name: Liu
historical_names.source: Gongyang Zhuan (公羊傳·桓公十一年, 701 BCE), noting Zheng's earlier settlement at Liu (留) before it was annexed by Chen.
historical_names.notes: Earlier Zheng town of Liu became Chenliu after annexation by Chen.

b_qiao.first_mention_attestation: Spring and Autumn Chu walled city of Qiao (譙城) and Qin Qiao County (譙縣) under Dang Commandery, listed in Book of Han (漢書·地理志).
b_qiao.etymology_analysis: From Classical Chinese 譙 (qiáo, 'watchtower'), the ancient name of Bozhou from Spring and Autumn Chu and Qin–Han Qiao County.

historical_names.name: Jiao
historical_names.source: Western Zhou / Spring and Autumn State of Jiao (焦國 / 焦城), annexed by Chen and later Chu, which built Qiao City (譙城).
historical_names.notes: Zhou-era Jiao preceded Chu's Qiao City and Qin Qiao County.

b_chengfu.first_mention_attestation: 533 BCE (Zuo Zhuan 左傳·昭公九年: '楚公子棄疾遷許于夷，實城父'), attesting Chengfu (城父) as a Chu city; later Qin/Han Chengfu County in Book of Han.
b_chengfu.etymology_analysis: From Classical Chinese 城父 (Chéngfù), an ancient Spring and Autumn Chu town name (replacing earlier Yi 夷) near Bozhou.

b_mengcheng.first_mention_attestation: 742 CE (Tang Tianbao 1), when Shansang County was renamed Mengcheng County (蒙城縣), recorded in Old Book of Tang (舊唐書·地理志).
b_mengcheng.etymology_analysis: From 蒙 (Méng, ancient regional name) + 城 (chéng, 'walled city'), coined in 742 CE under Tang Emperor Xuanzong; unrelated to the Mongols (who postdate 742 CE by centuries).

historical_names.name: Shansang
historical_names.source: Book of Han (漢書·地理志, 111 CE) lists Western Han Shansang County (山桑縣) under Pei Commandery, renamed Mengcheng in 742 CE.
historical_names.notes: Western Han through early Tang Shansang County was renamed Mengcheng County in 742 CE.

b_luyi.first_mention_attestation: Sui Dynasty Kaihuang 18th year (598 CE), when Wuping County was renamed Luyi County, recorded in Book of Sui (Suishu, Geography Treatise): 'Luyi, formerly called Wuping, renamed in Kaihuang 18th year.'
b_luyi.etymology_analysis: Luyi (鹿邑, 'Deer Town') was named in 598 CE during the Sui Dynasty, replacing the earlier Han/Northern Dynasties name Wuping (武平) and the Spring and Autumn / Han name Ku (苦). Traditional local lore links 'deer' to auspicious omens or hunting grounds near the Huiji/Guo river plain.

historical_names.name: Ku
historical_names.source: Shiji (Records of the Grand Historian) and Book of Han (Hanshu, Geography Treatise) attest Ku County (苦县) as Laozi's birthplace in the Spring and Autumn state of Chen.
historical_names.notes: Known as Ku (苦) from the Spring and Autumn period through Western Jin, and Wuping (武平) before 598 CE.

historical_names.name: Wuping
historical_names.source: Shiji (Records of the Grand Historian) and Book of Han (Hanshu, Geography Treatise) attest Ku County (苦县) as Laozi's birthplace in the Spring and Autumn state of Chen.
historical_names.notes: Known as Ku (苦) from the Spring and Autumn period through Western Jin, and Wuping (武平) before 598 CE.

b_shanfu.first_mention_attestation: Qin Dynasty (221 BCE), established as Shanfu County (单父县) in Dang Commandery, later attested in Book of Han (Hanshu, Geography Treatise) and Old Book of Tang (Jiu Tangshu).
b_shanfu.etymology_analysis: Shanfu (单父) is traditionally explained as named after Shan Juan (单卷), a legendary pre-dynastic sage said to be Emperor Shun's teacher who resided there. It was established as a formal county under the Qin Dynasty in 221 BCE and remained Shanfu County through the Tang Dynasty.

b_yutai.first_mention_attestation: Tang Dynasty Baoying 1st year (762 CE), when Fangyu County was renamed Yutai County, recorded in Old Book of Tang (Jiu Tangshu, Geography Treatise): 'In Baoying 1st year, changed to Yutai, named after Duke Yin of Lu's Fish-Viewing Terrace north of the city.'
b_yutai.etymology_analysis: Yutai (鱼台, 'Fish Terrace') was named in 762 CE after the nearby Guanyutai ('Fish-Viewing Terrace'), associated with Duke Yin of Lu's visit to Tang (棠) recorded in the Spring and Autumn Annals for 718 BCE.

historical_names.name: Tangyi
historical_names.source: Zuo Zhuan (Duke Yin 5th year, 718 BCE) records Tang (棠); Book of Han (Hanshu) attests Han Fangyu County (方与县).
historical_names.notes: Known as Tangyi in the Spring and Autumn period and Fangyu County from Qin/Han until 762 CE.

historical_names.name: Fangyu
historical_names.source: Zuo Zhuan (Duke Yin 5th year, 718 BCE) records Tang (棠); Book of Han (Hanshu) attests Han Fangyu County (方与县).
historical_names.notes: Known as Tangyi in the Spring and Autumn period and Fangyu County from Qin/Han until 762 CE.

b_songcheng.first_mention_attestation: Sui Dynasty Kaihuang 18th year (598 CE), when Suiyang County was renamed Songcheng County, recorded in Book of Sui (Suishu, Geography Treatise): 'Songcheng, formerly called Suiyang... renamed in Kaihuang 18th year.'
b_songcheng.etymology_analysis: Songcheng (宋城, 'Walled City of Song') was named in 598 CE after the ancient Zhou-dynasty State of Song (11th–3rd century BCE), whose capital lay at Shangqiu/Suiyang. Note that the current repo calque 'Song Dynasty' is anachronistic since the Song Dynasty (960 CE) took its name from Songzhou/Songcheng rather than vice versa.

historical_names.name: Shangqiu
historical_names.source: Zuo Zhuan (Duke Xiang 9th year, 564 BCE) attests Shangqiu; Qin Dynasty established Suiyang County (睢阳县) in 221 BCE, recorded in Shiji and Book of Han.
historical_names.notes: Called Shangqiu in the Spring and Autumn period and Suiyang from Qin until 598 CE.

historical_names.name: Suiyang
historical_names.source: Zuo Zhuan (Duke Xiang 9th year, 564 BCE) attests Shangqiu; Qin Dynasty established Suiyang County (睢阳县) in 221 BCE, recorded in Shiji and Book of Han.
historical_names.notes: Called Shangqiu in the Spring and Autumn period and Suiyang from Qin until 598 CE.

b_yucheng.first_mention_attestation: Sui Dynasty Kaihuang 16th year (596 CE), when the county was re-established and named Yucheng, recorded in Book of Sui (Suishu, Geography Treatise): 'Yucheng, called Xiao under Northern Wei, abolished under Northern Qi; established and renamed in Kaihuang 16th year.'
b_yucheng.etymology_analysis: Yucheng (虞城, 'Walled City of Yu') derives from the legendary Xia-era state of Youyu (有虞) associated with Shangjun, son of Emperor Shun. Qin established Yu County (虞县), which was renamed Yucheng County in 596 CE.

historical_names.name: Yu
historical_names.source: Qin Dynasty established Yu County (虞县), attested in Book of Han (Hanshu, Geography Treatise); Northern Wei called it Xiao County.
historical_names.notes: Known as Yu County in Qin/Han and Xiao in Northern Wei before 596 CE.

historical_names.name: Xiao
historical_names.source: Qin Dynasty established Yu County (虞县), attested in Book of Han (Hanshu, Geography Treatise); Northern Wei called it Xiao County.
historical_names.notes: Known as Yu County in Qin/Han and Xiao in Northern Wei before 596 CE.

b_xiayi.first_mention_attestation: Western Han Dynasty (c. 202 BCE), attested as Xiayi County (下邑县) under Liang Kingdom in Book of Han (Hanshu, Geography Treatise) and earlier as a Chu settlement in the Warring States period.
b_xiayi.etymology_analysis: Xiayi (下邑, 'Lower Settlement') was a Warring States Chu settlement and Han county name (originally centered near Dangshan, relocated to former Li County in the Northern Dynasties). It is a locator compound contrasting with an upper settlement.

b_xiangyi.first_mention_attestation: Qin Dynasty (221 BCE), established as Xiangyi County (襄邑县) in Dang Commandery, attested in Book of Han (Hanshu, Geography Treatise) and Book of Sui (Suishu).
b_xiangyi.etymology_analysis: Xiangyi (襄邑) was established as a county by the Qin Dynasty in 221 BCE and remained Xiangyi County under Songzhou during the Tang Dynasty before being elevated to Gongzhou and later renamed Suizhou (Sui County) in the Song and Jin dynasties.

b_ruyin.first_mention_attestation: Qin Dynasty (221 BCE), established as Ruyin County (汝阴县), later seat of Runan Commandery in Book of Han (Hanshu, Geography Treatise) and Yingzhou in Old Book of Tang (Jiu Tangshu).

morphemes.translation: south bank / shady side of a river

b_ruyin.etymology_analysis: Ruyin (汝阴, 'South/Shady Side of the Ru River') is a classic Chinese hydronymic locator compound indicating a settlement on the south bank (yin) of the Ru River. Established in the Qin Dynasty, it served as the seat of Yingzhou in the Tang Dynasty (modern Fuyang).

historical_names.name: Hu
historical_names.source: Zuo Zhuan attests the Zhou-era State of Hu (胡国) at this site before the Qin establishment of Ruyin County.
historical_names.notes: Site of the Spring and Autumn State of Hu prior to Qin Ruyin County.

b_shenqiu.first_mention_attestation: Tang Dynasty Shenlong 2nd year (706 CE), when Qinqiu was renamed Shenqiu, recorded in Old Book of Tang (Jiu Tangshu, Geography Treatise): 'Shenqiu, formerly called Qinqiu, unchanged through Sui; in Shenlong 2nd year, changed to Shenqiu.'
b_shenqiu.etymology_analysis: Shenqiu (沈丘, 'Mound/Ruins of Shen') was named in 706 CE after the ancient Zhou-era State of Shen (沈国), meaning the ruined mound of Shen.

historical_names.name: Qinqiu
historical_names.source: Spring and Autumn Chu settlement of Qinqiu (寝丘), attested as Qin County (寝县) in Book of Han (Hanshu) and Qinqiu through Sui.
historical_names.notes: Called Qinqiu / Qin County prior to 706 CE.

historical_names.name: Qin
historical_names.source: Spring and Autumn Chu settlement of Qinqiu (寝丘), attested as Qin County (寝县) in Book of Han (Hanshu) and Qinqiu through Sui.
historical_names.notes: Called Qinqiu / Qin County prior to 706 CE.

b_xiacai.first_mention_attestation: Spring and Autumn period, 493 BCE (27th year of King Jing of Zhou), when Wu relocated the State of Cai to Zhoulai and renamed it Xiacai (下蔡), recorded in Zuo Zhuan and Shiji.
b_xiacai.etymology_analysis: Xiacai (下蔡, 'Lower Cai') was named in 493 BCE when the State of Cai moved its capital downstream along the Huai/Ru basin to Zhoulai, distinguishing it from Shangcai ('Upper Cai'). It was a Qin/Han/Tang county (modern Fengtai County, Anhui).

historical_names.name: Zhoulai
historical_names.source: Zuo Zhuan (Duke Cheng 7th year, 584 BCE; Duke Zhao 4th year, 538 BCE) records the Zhou-era state and Chu town of Zhoulai (州来).
historical_names.notes: Known as Zhoulai (州来) before being renamed Xiacai in 493 BCE.

b_yingshang.first_mention_attestation: Sui Dynasty Daye 2nd year (606 CE), when the county was named Yingshang (颍上), recorded in Book of Sui (Suishu, Geography Treatise) and Old Book of Tang (Jiu Tangshu).
b_yingshang.etymology_analysis: Yingshang (颍上, 'Upon/Upper Ying River') is a directional/locator compound referring to its position along the Ying River (Taiping Huanyuji: 'named for resting on the upper reaches of the Ying River'). Established in 606 CE.

historical_names.name: Shen
historical_names.source: Book of Han (Hanshu, Geography Treatise) attests Han Shen County (慎县) at this site before 606 CE.
historical_names.notes: Called Shenyi / Shen County from Han until 606 CE.

historical_names.name: Shenyi
historical_names.source: Book of Han (Hanshu, Geography Treatise) attests Han Shen County (慎县) at this site before 606 CE.
historical_names.notes: Called Shenyi / Shen County from Han until 606 CE.

b_ruyang.first_mention_attestation: Sui Dynasty Daye 2nd year (606 CE), when Shangcai County at Xuanhu was renamed Ruyang County (汝阳县), recorded in Book of Sui (Suishu, Geography Treatise): 'Ruyang, formerly Shangcai... in early Daye, renamed Ruyang.'

morphemes.translation: north bank / sunny side of a river

b_ruyang.etymology_analysis: Ruyang (汝阳, 'North/Sunny Side of the Ru River') is a directional/locator compound. In the Tang Dynasty, Ruyang County was the seat of Caizhou (modern Runan County, Henan), renamed Runan only in 1913.

historical_names.name: Shangcai
historical_names.source: Book of Han (Hanshu, Geography Treatise) attests Shangcai County; Eastern Jin established Xuanhu Citadel (悬瓠城) as the seat of Runan Commandery.
historical_names.notes: Served as Shangcai / Xuanhu prior to being renamed Ruyang in 606 CE.

historical_names.name: Xuanhu
historical_names.source: Book of Han (Hanshu, Geography Treatise) attests Shangcai County; Eastern Jin established Xuanhu Citadel (悬瓠城) as the seat of Runan Commandery.
historical_names.notes: Served as Shangcai / Xuanhu prior to being renamed Ruyang in 606 CE.

b_xiping.first_mention_attestation: Western Han Dynasty, 4th year of Emperor Gaozu (203 BCE), when Xiping County (西平县) was established, attested in Book of Han (Hanshu, Geography Treatise).
b_xiping.etymology_analysis: Xiping (西平, 'Western Pacification') was established as a county in 203 BCE and belonged to Caizhou during the Tang Dynasty.

historical_names.name: Bai
historical_names.source: Spring and Autumn State of Bai (柏国) at this site prior to Western Han Xiping County.
historical_names.notes: Ancient State of Bai in the Spring and Autumn period.

b_pingyu.first_mention_attestation: Qin Dynasty (221 BCE), established as Pingyu County (平舆县) in Yingchuan Commandery, attested in Book of Han (Hanshu, Geography Treatise) and earlier as a Chu town (平舆邑).
b_pingyu.etymology_analysis: Pingyu (平舆) was a Warring States Chu settlement and Qin/Han/Tang county under Caizhou.

historical_names.name: Shen
historical_names.source: Western Zhou and Spring and Autumn State of Shen (沈国) prior to Chu Pingyu.
historical_names.notes: Territory of the ancient State of Shen.

b_xincai.first_mention_attestation: Qin Dynasty (221 BCE), established as Xincai County (新蔡县), attested in Book of Han (Hanshu, Geography Treatise) under Runan Commandery and Old Book of Tang (Jiu Tangshu).
b_xincai.etymology_analysis: Xincai (新蔡, 'New Cai') was named when the State of Cai expanded eastward to this site (distinct from Shangcai and Xiacai). Established as a county in Qin and attested continuously through the Tang Dynasty.

b_wanqiu.first_mention_attestation: Book of Odes (Shijing, Airs of Chen, 'Wanqiu', c. 7th century BCE): 'How you beat your drum, beneath Wanqiu'; later made the official county name in Sui Kaihuang (581 CE, Book of Sui).
b_wanqiu.etymology_analysis: Wanqiu (宛丘, 'Hollow-Topped Mound') is an ancient topographic proper name attested in the Book of Odes as the sacred mound of the State of Chen. In 581 CE, Sui renamed Chen County to Wanqiu County, which served as the seat of Chenzhou in the Tang Dynasty.

b_taikang.first_mention_attestation: Sui Dynasty Kaihuang 7th year (587 CE), when Yangxia County was renamed Taikang County, recorded in Book of Sui (Suishu, Geography Treatise): 'Taikang, formerly Yangxia... in Kaihuang 7th year changed to Taikang.'
b_taikang.etymology_analysis: Taikang (太康) was named in 587 CE after the legendary Xia Dynasty ruler Taikang, whose tomb was traditionally located southeast of the city.

historical_names.name: Yangxia
historical_names.source: Qin Shi Huang 23rd year (224 BCE) established Yangxia County (阳夏县), attested in Shiji and Book of Han (Hanshu).
historical_names.notes: Known as Yangxia County from 224 BCE until 587 CE.

b_xiangcheng_1.first_mention_attestation: Sui Dynasty Kaihuang 3rd year (583 CE), when Xiang County / Moling was established as Xiangcheng County (项城县), recorded in Book of Sui (Suishu, Geography Treatise) and Old Book of Tang.
b_xiangcheng_1.etymology_analysis: Xiangcheng (项城, 'Walled City of Xiang') derives from the Western Zhou and Spring and Autumn State of Xiang (项国). Renamed Xiangcheng in the Sui Dynasty and attached to Chenzhou in the Tang Dynasty.

historical_names.name: Xiang
historical_names.source: Qin Dynasty established Xiang County (项县), attested in Book of Han (Hanshu); Eastern Wei renamed it Moling (秣陵).
historical_names.notes: Known as Xiang County in Qin/Han and Moling in Eastern Wei prior to Sui Xiangcheng.

historical_names.name: Moling
historical_names.source: Qin Dynasty established Xiang County (项县), attested in Book of Han (Hanshu); Eastern Wei renamed it Moling (秣陵).
historical_names.notes: Known as Xiang County in Qin/Han and Moling in Eastern Wei prior to Sui Xiangcheng.

b_yiyang.first_mention_attestation: Cao Wei period (c. 220–265 CE), when Yiyang Commandery and Yiyang County (义阳县) were split from Nanyang Commandery, recorded in Old Book of Tang (Jiu Tangshu, Geography Treatise): 'Wei split Nanyang to establish Yiyang Commandery.'
b_yiyang.etymology_analysis: Yiyang (义阳) originated as Yiyang Township (义阳乡) of Ping氏 County in the Han Dynasty and became Yiyang Commandery/County under Cao Wei, serving as the seat of Shenzhou in the Tang Dynasty (renamed Xinyang in 976 CE due to Song Taizong's naming taboo).

b_luoshan.first_mention_attestation: Sui Dynasty Kaihuang 16th year (596 CE), when Luoshan County was split from Zhongshan County, recorded in Book of Sui (Suishu, Geography Treatise) and Old Book of Tang (Jiu Tangshu).
b_luoshan.etymology_analysis: Luoshan (罗山, 'Mount Luo') was established in 596 CE and named after Mount Xiaoluo (小罗山) in the southwest of the county.

historical_names.name: Meng
historical_names.source: Western Han established Meng County (鄳县) in Jiangxia Commandery (Book of Han); Liu Song split off Baocheng; Northern Qi merged them into Gao'an.
historical_names.notes: Part of Meng, Baocheng, and Gao'an counties before 596 CE.

historical_names.name: Baocheng
historical_names.source: Western Han established Meng County (鄳县) in Jiangxia Commandery (Book of Han); Liu Song split off Baocheng; Northern Qi merged them into Gao'an.
historical_names.notes: Part of Meng, Baocheng, and Gao'an counties before 596 CE.

historical_names.name: Gao'an
historical_names.source: Western Han established Meng County (鄳县) in Jiangxia Commandery (Book of Han); Liu Song split off Baocheng; Northern Qi merged them into Gao'an.
historical_names.notes: Part of Meng, Baocheng, and Gao'an counties before 596 CE.

b_zhongshan.first_mention_attestation: Early Sui Dynasty Kaihuang era (581–583 CE), when Qi'an County was renamed Zhongshan County, recorded in Book of Sui (Suishu, Geography Treatise): 'Zhongshan, formerly Meng; Northern Qi renamed it Qi'an... in early Kaihuang, renamed Zhongshan. Has Mount Zhong.'
b_zhongshan.etymology_analysis: Zhongshan (钟山, 'Bell Mountain') was a county under Shenzhou (Xinyang, Henan) during the Sui and Tang dynasties, named after the local Mount Zhong (钟山). Later merged into Xinyang County in the early Northern Song.

historical_names.name: Meng
historical_names.source: Book of Han (Hanshu, Geography Treatise) attests Han Meng County (鄳县); Northern Qi renamed it Qi'an (齐安).
historical_names.notes: Known as Meng County in Han and Qi'an in Northern Qi before Sui Kaihuang.

historical_names.name: Qi'an
historical_names.source: Book of Han (Hanshu, Geography Treatise) attests Han Meng County (鄳县); Northern Qi renamed it Qi'an (齐安).
historical_names.notes: Known as Meng County in Han and Qi'an in Northern Qi before Sui Kaihuang.

b_changshe.first_mention_attestation: Qin Dynasty (221 BCE), established as Changshe County (长社县), attested in Book of Han (Hanshu, Geography Treatise) and Old Book of Tang (Jiu Tangshu) as seat of Xuzhou.
b_changshe.etymology_analysis: Changshe (长社, 'Long Earth-Altar') was a Qin/Han county name; in 618–907 CE Tang Dynasty it served as the seat of Xuzhou (modern Changge, Henan).

b_fugou.first_mention_attestation: Western Han Dynasty, 11th year of Emperor Gaozu (196 BCE), when Fugou County (扶沟县) was established, attested in Book of Han (Hanshu, Geography Treatise).
b_fugou.etymology_analysis: Fugou (扶沟) was established in 196 BCE, traditionally named from the combination of Futing (扶亭) and the Kang Ditch (康沟) within its territory.

b_yangzhai.first_mention_attestation: Warring States period, 400 BCE (9th year of Marquess Jing of Han), when the State of Han made Yangzhai (阳翟) its capital, recorded in Shiji and Zhushu Jinian (Bamboo Annals).
b_yangzhai.etymology_analysis: Yangzhai (阳翟) was the capital of the Warring States State of Han from 400 BCE and later seat of Yingchuan Commandery in Qin and Han (modern Yuzhou, Henan).

historical_names.name: Li
historical_names.source: Spring and Autumn State of Zheng settlement of Liyi (栎邑), attested in Zuo Zhuan before 400 BCE.
historical_names.notes: Known as Liyi under Zheng before Han renamed it Yangzhai in 400 BCE.

historical_names.name: Liyi
historical_names.source: Spring and Autumn State of Zheng settlement of Liyi (栎邑), attested in Zuo Zhuan before 400 BCE.
historical_names.notes: Known as Liyi under Zheng before Han renamed it Yangzhai in 400 BCE.

b_wuyang.first_mention_attestation: Qin Dynasty (221 BCE), established as Wuyang County (舞阳县) in Yingchuan Commandery, attested in Shiji and Book of Han (Hanshu, Geography Treatise).

morphemes.translation: north bank / sunny side of a river

b_wuyang.etymology_analysis: Wuyang (舞阳, 'North/Sunny Side of the Wu River') is a directional/locator compound named for its location on the north bank of the Wu River (舞水). Re-established in Tang Kaiyuan 4th year (716 CE).

historical_names.name: Hebo
historical_names.source: Zhan Guo Ce (Strategies of the Warring States, Han I) mentions Hebo (合伯) in southern Wuyang.
historical_names.notes: Warring States settlement of Hebo prior to Qin Wuyang County.

b_luoyang.first_mention_attestation: Qin Dynasty (221 BCE), established as Luoyang County (洛阳县) under Sanchuan Commandery (earlier Zhou-era Luoyi/Chengzhou), attested in Shiji and Book of Han (Hanshu).

morphemes.translation: north bank / sunny side of a river

b_luoyang.etymology_analysis: Luoyang (洛阳, 'North/Sunny Side of the Luo River') is a directional/locator compound denoting its position north of the Luo River. Served as Eastern Capital (Dongdu) of the Tang Dynasty.

historical_names.name: Luoyi
historical_names.source: Western Zhou bronze inscriptions (He Zun, c. 1038 BCE) and Shangshu (Book of Documents) attest Luoyi (洛邑) and Chengzhou (成周).
historical_names.notes: Western and Eastern Zhou royal capitals Luoyi, Wangcheng, and Chengzhou.

historical_names.name: Chengzhou
historical_names.source: Western Zhou bronze inscriptions (He Zun, c. 1038 BCE) and Shangshu (Book of Documents) attest Luoyi (洛邑) and Chengzhou (成周).
historical_names.notes: Western and Eastern Zhou royal capitals Luoyi, Wangcheng, and Chengzhou.

historical_names.name: Wangcheng
historical_names.source: Western Zhou bronze inscriptions (He Zun, c. 1038 BCE) and Shangshu (Book of Documents) attest Luoyi (洛邑) and Chengzhou (成周).
historical_names.notes: Western and Eastern Zhou royal capitals Luoyi, Wangcheng, and Chengzhou.

b_yanshi.first_mention_attestation: Qin Dynasty (221 BCE), established as Yanshi County (偃师县) in Sanchuan Commandery after the conquest of Zhou, attested in Book of Han (Hanshu, Geography Treatise).
b_yanshi.etymology_analysis: Yanshi (偃师, 'Resting the Troops') is traditionally explained as commemorating King Wu of Zhou's victory over Shang, when he rested and disbanded his army ('息偃戎师') at this site.

historical_names.name: Xibo
historical_names.source: Early Shang capital site of Xibo (西亳) in Yanshi, attested in Shiji and Shangshu traditions.
historical_names.notes: Site of the early Shang capital Xibo.

b_fuchang.first_mention_attestation: Tang Dynasty Wude 1st year (618 CE), when Yiyang County was renamed Fuchang County, recorded in Old Book of Tang (Jiu Tangshu, Geography Treatise): 'In Wude 1st year, Yiyang Commandery was changed to Xiongzhou... and Yiyang was renamed Fuchang County.'
b_fuchang.etymology_analysis: Fuchang (福昌, 'Blessed and Prosperous') was named in 618 CE after the Sui-era Fuchang Palace (福昌宫) located there, replacing the older name Yiyang (modern Yiyang County, Henan).

historical_names.name: Yiyang
historical_names.source: Warring States Han town and Qin/Han Yiyang County (宜阳县), attested in Shiji and Book of Han (Hanshu).
historical_names.notes: Known as Yiyang County from Qin until 618 CE.

b_yique.first_mention_attestation: Warring States period, 293 BCE (Battle of Yique), recorded in Shiji (Records of the Grand Historian); established as Yique County in Sui Kaihuang 18th year (598 CE, Book of Sui).
b_yique.etymology_analysis: Yique (伊阙, 'Yi Gate') is the ancient name of the dramatic twin-peaked mountain gorge (Longmen) south of Luoyang through which the Yi River flows. Famous for the 293 BCE Battle of Yique and later made a Sui/Tang county name in 598 CE.

b_dengfeng.first_mention_attestation: Wu Zhou Dynasty Wansui Dengfeng 1st year (696 CE), when Wu Zetian renamed Songyang County to Dengfeng County, recorded in Old Book of Tang (Jiu Tangshu, Geography Treatise): 'In Dengfeng 1st year, 12th month, renamed Dengfeng County.'
b_dengfeng.etymology_analysis: Dengfeng (登封, 'Ascend and Perform Feng Sacrifices') was named in 696 CE by Empress Wu Zetian to commemorate ascending Mount Song (Central Peak) to perform the imperial Feng sacrifice.

historical_names.name: Chonggao
historical_names.source: Book of Han (Hanshu) attests Chonggao County (崇高县, 110 BCE); Book of Sui records Songyang County (嵩阳县, 605 CE).
historical_names.notes: Called Chonggao in Han and Songyang in Sui/early Tang before 696 CE.

historical_names.name: Songyang
historical_names.source: Book of Han (Hanshu) attests Chonggao County (崇高县, 110 BCE); Book of Sui records Songyang County (嵩阳县, 605 CE).
historical_names.notes: Called Chonggao in Han and Songyang in Sui/early Tang before 696 CE.

b_liang.first_mention_attestation: Qin Dynasty (221 BCE), established as Liang County (梁县) in Sanchuan Commandery, attested in Book of Han (Hanshu, Geography Treatise) and Old Book of Tang (Jiu Tangshu) as seat of Ruzhou.
b_liang.etymology_analysis: Liang (梁) was an ancient Spring and Autumn Chu settlement (梁邑) and a Qin/Han/Tang county serving as the seat of Ruzhou (modern Ruzhou, Henan).

b_xiangcheng.first_mention_attestation: Qin Dynasty, 2nd year of Ershi (208 BCE), when Xiang Yu besieged Xiangcheng (襄城), recorded in Shiji (Basic Annals of Xiang Yu) and Book of Han (Hanshu, Geography Treatise).
b_xiangcheng.etymology_analysis: Xiangcheng (襄城, 'Walled City of Xiang') is traditionally named after King Xiang of Zhou, who took refuge in this area during Prince Dai's rebellion and built a walled town.

historical_names.name: Fancheng
historical_names.source: Zuo Zhuan records the Zheng settlement of Nanfan / Fancheng (氾城) where King Xiang of Zhou resided in 636 BCE.
historical_names.notes: Known as Fancheng in the Spring and Autumn period.

b_ye_2.first_mention_attestation: Spring and Autumn period, 576 BCE (10th year of King Jian of Zhou), when Chu moved the State of Xu to Ye (叶), recorded in Zuo Zhuan; later enfeoffed to Shen Zhuliang (Lord of Ye) in 524 BCE.
b_ye_2.etymology_analysis: Ye (叶, historically pronounced Shè in this toponym) was a Spring and Autumn Chu settlement and Qin/Han/Tang county under Ruzhou (modern Ye County, Henan), famous for the Lord of Ye (叶公).

b_hongnong.first_mention_attestation: Western Han Dynasty Yuanding 3rd–4th year (114–113 BCE), when Hongnong County and Hongnong Commandery (弘农郡) were established by Emperor Wu of Han, recorded in Book of Han (Hanshu, Geography Treatise).
b_hongnong.etymology_analysis: Hongnong (弘农, 'Great Agriculture') was established in 114–113 BCE by Emperor Wu of Han near Hangu Pass and remained the seat of Guozhou (modern Lingbao, Henan) in the Tang Dynasty.

b_lushi.first_mention_attestation: Western Han Dynasty Yuanding 4th year (113 BCE), when Lushi County (卢氏县) was established under Hongnong Commandery, recorded in Book of Han (Hanshu, Geography Treatise).
b_lushi.etymology_analysis: Lushi (卢氏, 'Lu Clan') was established in 113 BCE and named after the ancient Lu clan (卢氏) or a Jin/Qin noble lineage settled in the Luo River valley.

historical_names.name: Xin
historical_names.source: Western Zhou territory of Xin (莘地) under the State of Guo, prior to Han Lushi County.
historical_names.notes: Known as Xin (莘地) of Guo in the Western Zhou period.

b_shan.first_mention_attestation: Warring States period, 390 BCE, when Shan County (陕县) was established (later governed by Sanchuan Commandery under Qin in 225 BCE and seat of Shanzhou in Tang), recorded in Shiji and Book of Han.
b_shan.etymology_analysis: Shan (陕) derives from the narrow Yellow River gorge and plateau pass (Shan Pass / Shanmo) on the southern bank of the Yellow River, which also gave its name to Shaanxi ('west of the Shan Pass').

b_lingbao.first_mention_attestation: Xin Tangshu (New Book of Tang, ch. 38, Dilizhi): Lingbao County (灵宝县) was renamed from Taolin County in Tianbao 1 (742 CE) after a Daoist 'numinous talisman' (灵符) was unearthed at Hangu Pass.
b_lingbao.etymology_analysis: Renamed from Taolin County to Lingbao in 742 CE under Emperor Xuanzong of Tang to commemorate the discovery of a Daoist 'numinous talisman' (灵符) at nearby Hangu Pass, evoking 'numinous treasure' (灵宝).

historical_names.name: Hongnong
historical_names.source: Hanshu (Book of Han, Dilizhi): Hongnong County established in 113 BCE (Yuanding 4); renamed Taolin County in 596 CE (Sui Kaihuang 16).
historical_names.notes: Hongnong was the Han-era commandery and county seat; Sui established Taolin County in 596 CE before the 742 CE renaming to Lingbao.

historical_names.name: Taolin
historical_names.source: Hanshu (Book of Han, Dilizhi): Hongnong County established in 113 BCE (Yuanding 4); renamed Taolin County in 596 CE (Sui Kaihuang 16).
historical_names.notes: Hongnong was the Han-era commandery and county seat; Sui established Taolin County in 596 CE before the 742 CE renaming to Lingbao.

b_baima.first_mention_attestation: Shiji & Hanshu (Dilizhi): Baima County (白马县) was a Qin/Han county in Dong Commandery (established 242 BCE), centered near the ancient Baima Ford (白马津) on the Yellow River.
b_baima.etymology_analysis: Named after Baima Ford (白马津, 'White Horse Ford') on the Yellow River, traditionally linked to ritual white-horse sacrifices or covenants at the crossing; served as the seat of Dong Commandery and later Hua Prefecture.

b_lingchang.first_mention_attestation: Suishu (Book of Sui, Dilizhi) & Yuanhe Junxian Tuzhi (ch. 8): Lingchang County (灵昌县) was established in Sui Kaihuang 16 (596 CE), taking its name from Lingchang Ford (灵昌津).
b_lingchang.etymology_analysis: Established in 596 CE under the Sui dynasty and named after Lingchang Ford (灵昌津) on the Yellow River; also gave its name to Lingchang Commandery (742–758 CE) during the Tang dynasty.

b_suanzao.first_mention_attestation: Shiji (ch. 69, Su Qin Liezhuan, compiled ca. 94 BCE) & Hanshu (Dilizhi): Suanzao (酸枣) is attested as a Warring States Wei town and Qin/Han county in Chenliu Commandery (also site of the 168 BCE Yellow River dike breach).
b_suanzao.etymology_analysis: Named for the abundance of wild sour jujube trees (Ziziphus jujuba var. spinosa) in the area; attested from the Warring States period through the Qin, Han, and Tang dynasties.

b_guancheng.first_mention_attestation: Suishu (Dilizhi) & Xin Tangshu (Dilizhi): Guancheng County (管城县) was established in Sui Kaihuang 16 (596 CE) as the seat of Guan Prefecture (later Zheng Prefecture).
b_guancheng.etymology_analysis: Named after the ancient Western Zhou fief of Guan (管), held by Guan Shu Xian, combined with cheng ('walled city'); established as a county in 596 CE.

historical_names.name: Guan
historical_names.source: Shiji (Zhou Benji / Guan-Cai Shijia): records the Western Zhou state of Guan (管) enfeoffed to Guan Shu.
historical_names.notes: Ancient Guan city predates the 596 CE Sui county establishment.

b_yangwu.first_mention_attestation: Shiji & Hanshu (Dilizhi): Yangwu County (阳武县) was established under the Qin dynasty and recorded in Shiji (e.g., Bolangsha in Yangwu, 218 BCE) and Hanshu as a county of Henan Commandery.
b_yangwu.etymology_analysis: Qin-era county name combining yang (sunny/south-facing, or north of a river) and wu (martial), an auspicious/military toponym.

b_xingyang.first_mention_attestation: Shiji (Qin Benji / Zhang Yi Liezhuan): Xingyang (荥阳) was built by the Warring States state of Han by ca. 320 BCE and captured by Qin in 249 BCE to form Sanchuan Commandery.
b_xingyang.etymology_analysis: Locator compound meaning 'north (yang) of Xing Marsh (荥泽)'; a strategic fortress town from the Warring States through the Qin, Han, and Tang dynasties.

b_xiapi.first_mention_attestation: Shiji & Hanshu (Dilizhi): Xiapi County (下邳县) was established under the Qin dynasty and is attested in Shiji (e.g., 202 BCE Han capture of Xiapi) and Hanshu.
b_xiapi.etymology_analysis: Directional/locator compound 'Lower Pi', named relative to Shangpi ('Upper Pi' in Shandong) after the ancient Zhou-era State of Pi.

b_suqian.first_mention_attestation: Xin Tangshu (Dilizhi) & Yuanhe Junxian Tuzhi (ch. 10): Renamed Suqian County (宿迁县) in Tang Baoying 1 (762 CE) from Suyu County to avoid the naming taboo of Emperor Daizong (Li Yu).
b_suqian.etymology_analysis: Adopted in 762 CE to replace Suyu (宿豫) due to imperial naming taboo on Yu (豫), alluding to the Spring and Autumn event where Song relocated (迁) the state of Su (宿) here.

historical_names.name: Suyu
historical_names.source: Shiji (Xiang Yu Benji) for Qin Xiaxiang County; Jinshu / Yuanhe Junxian Tuzhi for Suyu County (405 CE).
historical_names.notes: Qin Xiaxiang County was renamed Suyu in 405 CE under Eastern Jin, then Suqian in 762 CE.

historical_names.name: Xiaxiang
historical_names.source: Shiji (Xiang Yu Benji) for Qin Xiaxiang County; Jinshu / Yuanhe Junxian Tuzhi for Suyu County (405 CE).
historical_names.notes: Qin Xiaxiang County was renamed Suyu in 405 CE under Eastern Jin, then Suqian in 762 CE.

b_tancheng.first_mention_attestation: Hou Hanshu (Book of the Later Han): Records Wu Han capturing Tancheng (郯城, the walled city of Tan) in Jianwu 5 (29 CE); the older state/county name Tan (郯) is attested in Zuozhuan and Hanshu.
b_tancheng.etymology_analysis: Compound of the ancient Spring and Autumn state of Tan (郯) and cheng ('walled city'), referring to the ancient capital of Tan.

historical_names.name: Tan
historical_names.source: Shiji & Hanshu (Dilizhi): Tan County (郯县) was the Qin/Han seat of Donghai Commandery, preceded by the Zhou-era State of Tan.
historical_names.notes: The county was formally called Tan (郯县) in Qin, Han, and Tang, while the walled seat was referred to as Tancheng (郯城).

b_linhuai.first_mention_attestation: Yuanhe Junxian Tuzhi (ch. 10) & Xin Tangshu (Dilizhi): Linhuai County (临淮县) was established in Tang Chang'an 4 (704 CE) from two townships of Xucheng County, becoming the seat of Si Prefecture in 735 CE.
b_linhuai.etymology_analysis: Locator compound meaning 'overlooking the Huai River', established as a county in 704 CE at the junction of the Bian Canal and the Huai River (also echoing the Han-era Linhuai Commandery).

historical_names.name: Xu
historical_names.source: Hanshu (Dilizhi) & Yuanhe Junxian Tuzhi (ch. 10): notes Linhuai County was carved out of Han Xu County / Tang Xucheng County.
historical_names.notes: Carved from the southern boundary of Xucheng County in 704 CE.

historical_names.name: Xucheng
historical_names.source: Hanshu (Dilizhi) & Yuanhe Junxian Tuzhi (ch. 10): notes Linhuai County was carved out of Han Xu County / Tang Xucheng County.
historical_names.notes: Carved from the southern boundary of Xucheng County in 704 CE.

b_xucheng.first_mention_attestation: Xin Tangshu (Dilizhi) & Yuanhe Junxian Tuzhi (ch. 10): Xucheng County (徐城县) is attested under Si Prefecture by early Tang (618/621 CE, and Sui-era restructuring of Han Xu County).
b_xucheng.etymology_analysis: Named after the ancient State of Xu (徐国) and its capital Da Xucheng (大徐城), adding cheng ('walled city') to the earlier Han Xu County.

historical_names.name: Xu
historical_names.source: Hanshu (Dilizhi): Xu County (徐县) was the seat of Linhuai Commandery in Western Han.
historical_names.notes: Han Xu County succeeded the ancient State of Xu and was later renamed Xucheng County.

b_lianshui.first_mention_attestation: Suishu (Dilizhi) & Yuanhe Junxian Tuzhi (ch. 10): In Sui Kaihuang 5 (585 CE), Xiangbi County was renamed Lianshui County (涟水县) after the Lian River.
b_lianshui.etymology_analysis: Named directly after the Lian River (涟水) flowing through its territory when Xiangbi County was renamed in 585 CE.

historical_names.name: Xiangbi
historical_names.source: Songshu (Book of Song, Zhoujunzhi) & Yuanhe Junxian Tuzhi (ch. 10): Liu Song established Xiangbi County here before the 585 CE renaming.
historical_names.notes: Renamed from Xiangbi to Lianshui in 585 CE.

b_fuli.first_mention_attestation: Zhanguo Ce & Hanshu (Dilizhi): Fuli (符离) is attested in Zhanguo Ce as a Chu frontier pass and was established as Fuli County (符离县) under the Qin dynasty (belonging to Sishui/Pei Commandery).
b_fuli.etymology_analysis: Ancient Chu/Qin place name; classical commentators note fuli refers either to marsh reeds/plants or to an ancient frontier checkpoint.

b_hong.first_mention_attestation: Hanshu (Dilizhi, 2 CE Yuanshi census) & Xin Tangshu (Dilizhi): Hong County (虹县) is recorded in Hanshu under Pei Commandery (and re-established in Tang Wude 4, 621 CE).
b_hong.etymology_analysis: Ancient Han-era county name in Pei Commandery, revived in 621 CE under the Tang dynasty and later serving as the initial seat of Su Prefecture in 809 CE.

b_linhuan.first_mention_attestation: Suishu (Dilizhi) & Xin Tangshu (Dilizhi): Linhuan Commandery (临涣郡) was established in Southern Liang Putong 6 (525 CE), and Northern Qi renamed Huanbei County to Linhuan County (临涣县).
b_linhuan.etymology_analysis: Locator compound meaning 'overlooking the Huan River (涣水)', established during the Northern and Southern Dynasties on the site of Han-era Zhi County.

historical_names.name: Zhi
historical_names.source: Hanshu (Dilizhi) for Han Zhi County; Weishu (Dixingzhi) for Northern Wei Huanbei County.
historical_names.notes: Han Zhi County was renamed Huanbei by Northern Wei and then Linhuan by Northern Qi.

historical_names.name: Huanbei
historical_names.source: Hanshu (Dilizhi) for Han Zhi County; Weishu (Dixingzhi) for Northern Wei Huanbei County.
historical_names.notes: Han Zhi County was renamed Huanbei by Northern Wei and then Linhuan by Northern Qi.

b_qi.first_mention_attestation: Shiji (Chen She Shijia, ch. 48): Records Chen Sheng and Wu Guang's Dazexiang uprising in Qi County (蕲县) in 209 BCE; also listed in Hanshu (Dilizhi) under Pei Commandery.
b_qi.etymology_analysis: Qin-era county name, traditionally associated with the qi aromatic herb or ancient Chu place naming; famous as the site of the 209 BCE Dazexiang uprising.

b_pengcheng.first_mention_attestation: Shiji (Xiang Yu Benji) & Hanshu (Dilizhi): Pengcheng (彭城) was a Qin county in Sishui Commandery and served as Xiang Yu's Western Chu capital in 206 BCE.
b_pengcheng.etymology_analysis: Named after the legendary ancient polity of Dapeng (大彭) associated with Pengzu, combined with cheng ('walled city').

b_teng.first_mention_attestation: Spring and Autumn Annals / Zuo Zhuan (Yingong 7, 716 BCE: '滕侯卒'), Mencius & Suishu (Dilizhi): Zhou-era State of Teng (滕國), later established as Teng County (滕縣) under Qin.
b_teng.etymology_analysis: Named after the Western Zhou and Spring and Autumn State of Teng (滕国), whose name is glossed in Shuowen as 'gushing/surging water'.

b_pei.first_mention_attestation: Shiji (Gaozu Benji) & Hanshu (Dilizhi): Pei County (沛县) was established by Chu/Qin in Sishui Commandery and is famous as the home county of Han founder Liu Bang ('Lord of Pei', 209 BCE).
b_pei.etymology_analysis: Derived from the low-lying marshland (Pei Marsh, 沛泽) of the Sishui/Huai basin; attested since the Warring States and Qin periods.

b_xiao.first_mention_attestation: Zuo Zhuan (Zhuanggong 12, 682 BCE) & Hanshu (Dilizhi): originally the Spring and Autumn State of Xiao (蕭國), later established as Xiao County (蕭縣) under the Qin dynasty in Sishui Commandery.
b_xiao.etymology_analysis: Named after the Spring and Autumn state of Xiao (萧国), a vassal state of Song annexed by Chu in 597 BCE, and maintained as Xiao County from Qin through Tang.

b_qushan.first_mention_attestation: Suishu (Dilizhi) & Xin Tangshu (Dilizhi): Northern Zhou renamed Qu County to Qushan County (朐山县) in Jiande 6 (577 CE) after Mount Qu.
b_qushan.etymology_analysis: Named directly after Mount Qu (朐山) near Haizhou (modern Lianyungang) when Qu County was renamed in 577 CE.

historical_names.name: Qu
historical_names.source: Shiji (Qin Shihuang Benji) & Hanshu (Dilizhi): Qin established Qu County (朐县), where Qin Shihuang erected a stone gate.
historical_names.notes: Qin/Han Qu County was renamed Qushan County in 577 CE.

b_huairen.first_mention_attestation: Suishu (Dilizhi) & Xin Tangshu (Dilizhi): Huairen County (怀仁县) was established during the Northern and Southern Dynasties and consolidated under Sui Kaihuang 3 (583 CE) in Hai Prefecture.
b_huairen.etymology_analysis: Auspicious Confucian administrative name ('cherishing benevolence'), used for the county in Hai Prefecture (modern Ganyu) from the 6th century until 1167 CE.

b_muyang.first_mention_attestation: Weishu (Dixingzhi) & Suishu (Dilizhi): Muyang/Shuyang County (沭阳县) was established in Eastern Wei (by 549 CE) and retained under Northern Qi, Northern Zhou, Sui, and Tang.
b_muyang.etymology_analysis: Locator compound meaning 'north (yang) of the Shu River (沭水)'; note that in modern Mandarin the river/county character 沭 is read Shù, though historically also glossed as Mù.

b_linyi.first_mention_attestation: Hanshu (Dilizhi, 2 CE Yuanshi census): Lists Linyi County (临沂县) under Donghai Commandery; later served as the seat of Yi Prefecture in Tang.
b_linyi.etymology_analysis: Locator compound meaning 'overlooking the Yi River (沂水)', attested since Western Han.

b_xintai.first_mention_attestation: Jinshu (Dilizhi) & West Jin administrative records: Dongpingyang County was renamed Xintai County (新泰县) in the Western Jin Taishi era (265–274 CE) on the proposal of Yang Hu.

natural_proper_name.name: Mount Xinfu & Mount Tai (新甫山、泰山)

b_xintai.etymology_analysis: Portmanteau coined by Western Jin statesman Yang Hu by combining the first characters of Mount Xinfu (新甫山) and Mount Tai (泰山), rather than 'New Supreme Peace'.

historical_names.name: Dongpingyang
historical_names.source: Hanshu (Dilizhi): Lists Dongpingyang County under Taishan Commandery.
historical_names.notes: Han Dongpingyang / Cao Wei Pingyang was renamed Xintai in early Western Jin.

historical_names.name: Pingyang
historical_names.source: Hanshu (Dilizhi): Lists Dongpingyang County under Taishan Commandery.
historical_names.notes: Han Dongpingyang / Cao Wei Pingyang was renamed Xintai in early Western Jin.

b_fei.first_mention_attestation: Zuo Zhuan (Xigong 1, 659 BCE: '公賜季友汶陽之田及費') & Hanshu (Dilizhi, 2 CE): attested as the Spring and Autumn Lu fief of Fei (費邑), later Fei County under Donghai Commandery.
b_fei.etymology_analysis: Named after the Spring and Autumn Lu fief of Fei (费邑, held by the Jisun clan) and earlier Bi (鄪); established as Fei County in Western Han.

b_yishui.first_mention_attestation: Suishu (Dilizhi) & Xin Tangshu (Dilizhi): Yishui County (沂水县) was established in Sui Kaihuang 16 (596 CE) in Langya Commandery / Yi Prefecture.
b_yishui.etymology_analysis: Named directly after the Yi River (沂水), which flows through the county; established in 596 CE.

historical_names.name: Dongguan
historical_names.source: Hanshu (Dilizhi): Lists Dongguan County under Langya Commandery (seat in modern Yishui).
historical_names.notes: Han-era Dongguan County preceded the 596 CE Sui creation of Yishui County.

b_cheng.first_mention_attestation: Hanshu (Dilizhi, 2 CE Yuanshi census) & Xin Tangshu (Dilizhi): Cheng County (承县) was established in Han under Donghai Commandery, became seat of Lanling Commandery in 291 CE, and belonged to Yi Prefecture in Tang.
b_cheng.etymology_analysis: Han-era county name in Donghai Commandery (modern Yicheng District, Zaozhuang), restored as Cheng County in early Tang after a brief Sui renaming to Lanling.

b_zhucheng.first_mention_attestation: Suishu (Dilizhi) & Xin Tangshu (Dilizhi): In Sui Kaihuang 18 (598 CE), Dongwu County was renamed Zhucheng County (诸城县), serving as the seat of Gaomi Commandery / Mi Prefecture.
b_zhucheng.etymology_analysis: Named after the ancient Spring and Autumn settlement of Zhu (诸) combined with cheng ('walled city'), when Dongwu County was renamed in 598 CE.

historical_names.name: Dongwu
historical_names.source: Hanshu (Dilizhi): Lists Dongwu County under Langya Commandery.
historical_names.notes: Han/Wei/Jin Dongwu County was renamed Zhucheng County in 598 CE.

b_gaomi.first_mention_attestation: Shiji (Huaiyin Hou Liezhuan) & Hanshu (Dilizhi): Gaomi (高密) was established as a Qin county and appears in Shiji in the 203 BCE Wei River campaign.
b_gaomi.etymology_analysis: Warring States Qi and Qin-era county name meaning 'high and dense' (or linked to the Mi region/river); served as capital of Gaomi State in Western Han.

b_jiaoxi.first_mention_attestation: Suishu (Dilizhi) & Xin Tangshu (Dilizhi): Jiaoxi County (胶西县) was established in Sui (absorbing Qianzou County by Daye, ca. 606 CE) and merged into Gaomi in Tang Wude 6 (623 CE).
b_jiaoxi.etymology_analysis: Directional/locator compound meaning 'west of the Jiao River (胶水)', echoing the Han-era Jiaoxi Commandery/Kingdom.

historical_names.name: Qianzou
historical_names.source: Hanshu (Dilizhi): Lists Qin/Han Qianzou County under Langya Commandery.
historical_names.notes: Qianzou County was merged into Sui Jiaoxi County at the start of the Daye era.

b_ju.first_mention_attestation: Spring and Autumn Annals / Zuo Zhuan (Yingong 2, 721 BCE: '莒人入向'), Shiji & Hanshu (Dilizhi): Zhou-era State of Ju (莒國), later established as Ju County (莒縣) under Qin and seat of Chengyang Commandery in Han.
b_ju.etymology_analysis: Named after the Spring and Autumn and Warring States State of Ju (莒国), maintained as Ju County from Qin through the Tang dynasty.

b_anqiu.first_mention_attestation: Shiji & Hanshu (Dilizhi): Western Han created the Marquisate of Anqiu (安丘侯) in 199 BCE and formally established Anqiu County (安丘县) in 148 BCE.
b_anqiu.etymology_analysis: Auspicious Han-era marquisate and county name ('pacified hill') established on the ancient Quqiu (渠丘) territory.

b_xiaqiu.first_mention_attestation: Hanshu (Dilizhi & Wangzi Hou Biao): Xiaqiu (瑕丘) was enfeoffed as a Lu prince's marquisate in Yuanshou/Yuanshuo 3 (126 BCE) and recorded as Xiaqiu County under Shanyang Commandery; later seat of Yan Prefecture in Tang.
b_xiaqiu.etymology_analysis: Derived from the pre-Qin Lu settlement of Fuxia (负瑕) combined with qiu ('hill'); served as the seat of Yan Prefecture during the Tang dynasty.

b_laiwu.first_mention_attestation: Hanshu (Dilizhi, 2 CE Yuanshi census): Lists Laiwu County (莱芜县) under Taishan Commandery, named after the Laiwu Valley (莱芜谷).
b_laiwu.etymology_analysis: Named after Laiwu Valley (莱芜谷), where, according to tradition, the people of the defeated State of Lai fled in the Spring and Autumn period, leaving overgrown settlements.

b_qianfeng.first_mention_attestation: Old Book of Tang (Jiu Tangshu, juan 38): in 666 CE (Qianfeng 1), Emperor Gaozong of Tang performed the Fengshan sacrifices at Mount Tai and renamed Bocheng County to Qianfeng County (乾封县).
b_qianfeng.etymology_analysis: Named in 666 CE to commemorate Emperor Gaozong's Fengshan ritual at Mount Tai, matching the new era name Qianfeng (乾封). Reverted to Bocheng in 668 CE and restored as Qianfeng in 705 CE.

historical_names.name: Boyang
historical_names.source: Old Book of Tang (juan 38) and Tai'an historical records: Qin dynasty Boyang County (-221 BCE), Han Bo County, Sui Bocheng County (596 CE).
historical_names.notes: Located at the southern foot of Mount Tai (modern Tai'an, Shandong).

historical_names.name: Bo
historical_names.source: Old Book of Tang (juan 38) and Tai'an historical records: Qin dynasty Boyang County (-221 BCE), Han Bo County, Sui Bocheng County (596 CE).
historical_names.notes: Located at the southern foot of Mount Tai (modern Tai'an, Shandong).

historical_names.name: Bocheng
historical_names.source: Old Book of Tang (juan 38) and Tai'an historical records: Qin dynasty Boyang County (-221 BCE), Han Bo County, Sui Bocheng County (596 CE).
historical_names.notes: Located at the southern foot of Mount Tai (modern Tai'an, Shandong).

b_fuqu.first_mention_attestation: Zuo Zhuan (Dinggong 4, 506 BCE) and Records of the Grand Historian (Shiji, Lu Zhougong Shijia): records the Zhou enfeoffment of Duke of Zhou's son Boqin at Qufu (曲阜), capital of the State of Lu.
b_fuqu.etymology_analysis: Corresponds to Qufu (曲阜; rendered as Fuqu in the input). According to the Book of Han (Hanshu), the name derives from a winding earthen mound stretching seven to eight li east of the ancient city of Lu.

historical_names.name: Yan
historical_names.source: Shang dynasty oracle bone inscriptions and traditional historiography (modern Qufu was the Shang-era polity of Yan prior to the Zhou conquest).
historical_names.notes: Tradition also associates the site with the legendary Shaohao's Mound (少昊之墟).

b_zou.first_mention_attestation: Warring States records (Mencius, Yuanhe Junxian Tuzhi juan 10): Duke Mu of Lu (r. 416–377 BCE) renamed the State of Zhu (邾) to Zou (邹) in the mid-4th century BCE, and Han established Zou County (驺县).

morphemes.translation: state/clan name Zou (variant of Zhu 邾)

b_zou.etymology_analysis: Derived from the ancient State of Zhu (邾), whose name was changed to Zou (邹/驺) under Duke Mu of Lu during the Warring States period; Yuanhe Junxian Tuzhi also connects it to nearby Mount Zou (邹山).

historical_names.name: Zhu
historical_names.source: Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu, Yin 1, 722 BCE): earliest contemporary chronicle attestation of the State of Zhu.
historical_names.notes: Birthplace of Mencius (modern Zoucheng, Shandong).

historical_names.name: Zhulou
historical_names.source: Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu, Yin 1, 722 BCE): earliest contemporary chronicle attestation of the State of Zhu.
historical_names.notes: Birthplace of Mencius (modern Zoucheng, Shandong).

b_jiyin.first_mention_attestation: Book of Han (Hanshu, juan 28): Emperor Jing of Han established Jiyin Kingdom (济阴国, later Jiyin Commandery) in 144 BCE; Sui dynasty later established Jiyin County in 586 CE.
b_jiyin.etymology_analysis: Locator compound meaning 'south (shady) side of the Ji River' (济水之阴). First attested as a Han kingdom/commandery in 144 BCE and as a county seat in 586 CE.

b_nanhua.first_mention_attestation: Old Book of Tang (Jiu Tangshu, juan 38): in 742 CE (Tianbao 1), Emperor Xuanzong of Tang renamed Lihu County (离狐县) to Nanhua County (南华县).
b_nanhua.etymology_analysis: Renamed in 742 CE in honor of Zhuangzi (posthumously titled Nanhua Zhenren, 'Perfected Person of Nanhua', and his text the Nanhua Zhenjing) during Emperor Xuanzong's Daoist reforms.

historical_names.name: Lihu
historical_names.source: Book of Han (Hanshu, juan 28) and Old Book of Tang (juan 38): Lihu County was established in the Western Han dynasty.
historical_names.notes: Located in modern Dongming / Heze area, southwestern Shandong.

b_yuanju.first_mention_attestation: Book of Han (Hanshu, juan 28) and historical county records: Yuanju County (冤句县 / 宛句县) was established in 220 BCE (27th year of King Zheng of Qin).
b_yuanju.etymology_analysis: Ancient Qin-Han county in Caozhou (modern Heze, Shandong), written 冤句 or 宛句 (pronounced Yuānqú). Famous as the hometown of late-Tang rebel leader Huang Chao.

b_kaocheng.first_mention_attestation: Book of the Later Han (Hou Hanshu): during the Eastern Han dynasty (under Emperor Zhang, r. 75–88 CE), Zi County (菑县) was renamed Kaocheng County (考城县).
b_kaocheng.etymology_analysis: Eastern Han renaming of Western Han Zi County (菑县), traditionally attributed to Emperor Zhang honoring filial piety in the district; later part of Caozhou in Tang.

historical_names.name: Zi
historical_names.source: Book of Han (Hanshu, juan 28): Western Han Zi County (菑县), briefly renamed Jiagu (嘉谷) under Xin dynasty.
historical_names.notes: Merged with Lanfeng in 1954 to form modern Lankao County, Henan.

historical_names.name: Jiagu
historical_names.source: Book of Han (Hanshu, juan 28): Western Han Zi County (菑县), briefly renamed Jiagu (嘉谷) under Xin dynasty.
historical_names.notes: Merged with Lanfeng in 1954 to form modern Lankao County, Henan.

b_puyang.first_mention_attestation: Records of the Grand Historian (Shiji, Annals of Qin Shi Huang): in 242 BCE, Qin conquered Wei's territory and established Dongjun (Eastern Commandery) centered at Puyang (濮阳).
b_puyang.etymology_analysis: Locator compound meaning 'north (sunny) bank of the Pu River' (濮水之阳). Attested from the late Warring States / Qin conquest of 242 BCE.

historical_names.name: Diqiu
historical_names.source: Zuo Zhuan (Xi 31, 629 BCE): State of Wey moved its capital to Diqiu (帝丘), on the site of later Puyang.
historical_names.notes: Ancient capital of the State of Wey during the Spring and Autumn period.

b_juancheng.first_mention_attestation: Spring and Autumn Annals / Zuo Zhuan (Zhuanggong 14, 680 BCE: '會齊侯...於鄄') & Hanshu (juan 28): attested as Juan (鄄) of Wey in the Spring and Autumn period, later designated Juancheng County (鄄城縣) by Qin and Western Han.
b_juancheng.etymology_analysis: Named after the Spring and Autumn settlement of Juan (鄄邑) in the State of Wey, formalized as Juancheng ('Walled City of Juan') in Qin and Western Han.

b_leize.first_mention_attestation: Book of Sui (Suishu, juan 30) and Old Book of Tang (juan 38): in 596 CE (Kaihuang 16 of Sui), Leize County (雷泽县) was established on the former site of Chengyang County.
b_leize.etymology_analysis: Named after the ancient Leize ('Thunder Marsh'), which is itself attested in pre-Qin texts (Shang Shu: Yu Gong and Shiji). The county of Leize was founded in 596 CE.

historical_names.name: Chengyang
historical_names.source: Book of Sui (juan 30) and Book of Han (juan 28): previously Western Han Chengyang County (成阳县).
historical_names.notes: Located in modern Juancheng / Heze area, Shandong.

b_licheng.first_mention_attestation: Book of Han (Hanshu, juan 28) and historical records of Jinan: Licheng County (历城县) was established in 153 BCE (4th year of Emperor Jing of Han).
b_licheng.etymology_analysis: Named 'Walled City of Mount Li' after Mount Li (历山, modern Thousand Buddha Mountain) to its south. Became the seat of Jinan Commandery in the Western Jin dynasty.

historical_names.name: Luo
historical_names.source: Zuo Zhuan (Huan 18, 694 BCE) for Luo (泺邑), and Warring States / Qin records for Lixia (历下邑/历下城).
historical_names.notes: Core historic county of Jinan, Shandong.

historical_names.name: Lixia
historical_names.source: Zuo Zhuan (Huan 18, 694 BCE) for Luo (泺邑), and Warring States / Qin records for Lixia (历下邑/历下城).
historical_names.notes: Core historic county of Jinan, Shandong.

b_linji.first_mention_attestation: Book of Sui (Suishu, juan 30) and Old Book of Tang (juan 38): established in 586 CE as Chaoyang County and renamed Linji County (临济县) in 596 CE (Kaihuang 16 of Sui).
b_linji.etymology_analysis: Locator compound meaning 'overlooking the Ji River' (临济水), assigned in 596 CE under the Sui dynasty.

historical_names.name: Jian
historical_names.source: Book of Han (juan 28) for Han Jian County (菅县) and Book of Sui (juan 30) for Sui Chaoyang County (586 CE).
historical_names.notes: Located in modern Zhangqiu District, Jinan, Shandong.

historical_names.name: Chaoyang
historical_names.source: Book of Han (juan 28) for Han Jian County (菅县) and Book of Sui (juan 30) for Sui Chaoyang County (586 CE).
historical_names.notes: Located in modern Zhangqiu District, Jinan, Shandong.

b_zhangqiu.first_mention_attestation: Book of Sui (Suishu, juan 30) and Old Book of Tang (juan 38): in 596 CE (Kaihuang 16 of Sui), Gaotang County was renamed Zhangqiu County (章丘县).
b_zhangqiu.etymology_analysis: Named in 596 CE after the local Zhangqiu hill/mound north of the county seat; succeeded earlier Yangqiu and Gaotang counties.

historical_names.name: Yangqiu
historical_names.source: Book of Han (juan 28): Western Han Yangqiu County (阳丘县) established in 153 BCE; Liu Song later named it Gaotang.
historical_names.notes: Modern Zhangqiu District, Jinan, Shandong.

historical_names.name: Gaotang
historical_names.source: Book of Han (juan 28): Western Han Yangqiu County (阳丘县) established in 153 BCE; Liu Song later named it Gaotang.
historical_names.notes: Modern Zhangqiu District, Jinan, Shandong.

b_changqing.first_mention_attestation: Book of Sui (Suishu, juan 30) and Old Book of Tang (juan 38): Changqing County (长清县) was established in 594 CE (Kaihuang 14 of Sui) from part of Lu County.
b_changqing.etymology_analysis: Named in 594 CE after the Qi Great Wall (齐长城, 'Chang') and the Qing River (清水, 'Qing') passing through the territory.

historical_names.name: Lu
historical_names.source: Book of Han (juan 28) and Changqing historical records: territory belonged to Western Han Lu County (卢县).
historical_names.notes: Modern Changqing District, Jinan, Shandong.

b_xuchang.first_mention_attestation: Book of Han (Hanshu, juan 28) and Xuchang County records: Xuchang County (须昌县) was established in the Qin dynasty (221 BCE) under Xue Commandery and continued under Western Han.
b_xuchang.etymology_analysis: Derived from the ancient Spring and Autumn polity of Xuju (须句), combined with the auspicious element Chang ('prosperous'). Seat of Yunzhou in Tang; renamed Xucheng in 923 CE.

historical_names.name: Xuju
historical_names.source: Spring and Autumn Annals / Zuo Zhuan (Xi 21, 639 BCE): capital of the ancient Wind-clan State of Xuju.
historical_names.notes: Submerged under Dongping Lake in 1000 CE; distinct from Xuchang in Henan.

b_donge.first_mention_attestation: Book of Han (Hanshu, juan 28) and Dong'e County records: Qin dynasty first designated the town Dong'e (东阿) under Dongjun (221 BCE), and Han established Dong'e County.
b_donge.etymology_analysis: Directional compound ('East E') distinguishing the Qi town of E (阿) from western localities; attested from the Qin dynasty (221 BCE).

historical_names.name: Ke
historical_names.source: Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu, Zhuang 13, 681 BCE) for Ke (柯), later called E (阿) in the Warring States period.
historical_names.notes: Famous for the Covenant of Ke in 681 BCE and Ejiao (Dong'e donkey-hide gelatin).

historical_names.name: E
historical_names.source: Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu, Zhuang 13, 681 BCE) for Ke (柯), later called E (阿) in the Warring States period.
historical_names.notes: Famous for the Covenant of Ke in 681 BCE and Ejiao (Dong'e donkey-hide gelatin).

b_juye.first_mention_attestation: Book of Han (Hanshu, juan 28) and Juye County records: Juye County (钜野县 / 巨野县) was established in the early Western Han dynasty under Shanyang Commandery.
b_juye.etymology_analysis: Named after the great ancient marshland Dayeze / Juye ('Great Wilderness Marsh', 大野泽), attested in Erya and Zuo Zhuan (where Duke Ai of Lu captured a qilin in 481 BCE).

b_zhongdu.first_mention_attestation: Book of Rites (Liji) and Records of the Grand Historian (Shiji, Confucius): records that Duke Ding of Lu appointed Confucius as magistrate of Zhongdu (中都宰) around 500 BCE; Tang later renamed Pinglu County to Zhongdu in 742 CE.
b_zhongdu.etymology_analysis: Directional/positional compound ('Middle Town/Capital') of the State of Lu where Confucius served as magistrate c. 500 BCE. In Han it became Dongpinglu, and in 742 CE Tang restored the name Zhongdu.

b_penglai.first_mention_attestation: Old Book of Tang (Jiu Tangshu, juan 38) and Penglai historical records: Tang established Penglai Garrison (蓬莱镇) in 634 CE (Zhenguan 8) and elevated it to Penglai County (蓬莱县) in 707 CE (Shenlong 3).
b_penglai.etymology_analysis: Named after the mythical island-mountain Mount Penglai in the Bohai Sea, which Emperor Wu of Han sought from a coastal fortress here; formalized as a Tang garrison in 634 CE and county in 707 CE.

historical_names.name: Huang
historical_names.source: Old Book of Tang (juan 38): previously part of Qin-Han Huang County (黄县).
historical_names.notes: Seat of Dengzhou from 707 CE onward.

b_muping.first_mention_attestation: Book of Han (Hanshu, juan 28): Muping County (牟平县) is attested in Western Han under Donglai Commandery; Tang re-established it at the old Dongmou seat in 665 CE.
b_muping.etymology_analysis: Named after the level plain (平) on the sunny southern side of Mount Mu (牟山) in the Jiaodong Peninsula; attested as a county in Western Han.

historical_names.name: Mou
historical_names.source: Muping historical records: Spring and Autumn State of Mou (牟国) and Han Dongmou County at the Tang seat.
historical_names.notes: Tang relocated Muping County to the former Dongmou city in 665 CE.

historical_names.name: Dongmou
historical_names.source: Muping historical records: Spring and Autumn State of Mou (牟国) and Han Dongmou County at the Tang seat.
historical_names.notes: Tang relocated Muping County to the former Dongmou city in 665 CE.

b_wendeng.first_mention_attestation: Taiping Huanyu Ji and Wendeng historical records: in 568 CE (Tiantong 4 of Northern Qi), Wendeng County (文登县) was created from parts of Muping and Guanyang.
b_wendeng.etymology_analysis: Named after Mount Wendeng (文登山), where according to Taiping Huanyu Ji Qin Shi Huang summoned scholars ('wen') to ascend ('deng') the mountain east of the city to praise his achievements.

historical_names.name: Buye
historical_names.source: Book of Han (juan 28): territory belonged to Western Han Buye (不夜) and Changyang counties, later Muping and Guanyang.
historical_names.notes: Easternmost tip of the Shandong Peninsula (modern Wendeng District, Weihai).

historical_names.name: Muping
historical_names.source: Book of Han (juan 28): territory belonged to Western Han Buye (不夜) and Changyang counties, later Muping and Guanyang.
historical_names.notes: Easternmost tip of the Shandong Peninsula (modern Wendeng District, Weihai).

historical_names.name: Guanyang
historical_names.source: Book of Han (juan 28): territory belonged to Western Han Buye (不夜) and Changyang counties, later Muping and Guanyang.
historical_names.notes: Easternmost tip of the Shandong Peninsula (modern Wendeng District, Weihai).

b_huang.first_mention_attestation: Book of Han (Hanshu, juan 28) and Huang County records: Qin dynasty established Huang County (黄县) under Qi Commandery (221 BCE); continued as the seat of Donglai Commandery in Eastern Han.
b_huang.etymology_analysis: Ancient Qin-Han county in Jiaodong (modern Longkou, Shandong), named after the local Huang settlement/polity. Renamed Penglai in 707 CE and re-created as a separate Huang County in 712 CE.

b_ye_1.first_mention_attestation: Book of Han (Hanshu, juan 28): Ye County (掖县, written 夜 in Qin) was established in the Western Han dynasty as the primary county of Donglai Commandery.
b_ye_1.etymology_analysis: Ancient Western Han county (modern Laizhou, Shandong), written 夜 in Qin and 掖 in Han; seat of Laizhou / Donglai Commandery in Sui and Tang.

b_jiaoshui.first_mention_attestation: Book of Sui (Suishu, juan 30) and Old Book of Tang (juan 38): in 601 CE (Renshou 1 of Sui), Changguang County was renamed Jiaoshui County (胶水县) to avoid the naming taboo of Yang Guang.
b_jiaoshui.etymology_analysis: Named directly after the Jiao River (胶水, already mentioned in Book of Han) when Sui renamed Changguang County in 601 CE to avoid Yang Guang's personal name.

historical_names.name: Changguang
historical_names.source: Book of Sui (juan 30) and Book of Han (juan 28): originally Changguang County (长广县) in Western Han.
historical_names.notes: Predecessor of modern Pingdu, Shandong.

b_changyang.first_mention_attestation: Book of Han (Hanshu, juan 28) and Qin sealing clay records (Jimo Commandery): Changyang County (昌阳县) was established in Qin (221 BCE) and continued in Western Han under Donglai Commandery.
b_changyang.etymology_analysis: Locator compound meaning 'sunny/north side of the Chang River' (昌水之阳), attested from the Qin and Western Han dynasties (modern Laiyang, Shandong).

b_jimo.first_mention_attestation: Strategies of the Warring States (Zhanguo Ce), Discourses of the States (Guoyu), and Shiji: Jimo (即墨) is attested as a major Qi commercial city in the Warring States period (4th century BCE) and became a Qin county.
b_jimo.etymology_analysis: Locator compound meaning 'near/approaching the Mo River' (地临墨水河而得名), famous for Tian Dan's defense of Qi in 279 BCE.

b_yidu_2.first_mention_attestation: Book of Han (Hanshu): in 127 BCE (Yuanshuo 2 of Emperor Wu of Han), Liu Hu, son of the King of Zichuan, was enfeoffed as Marquis of Yidu (益都侯); later re-established as Yidu County in Cao Wei and Liu Song.
b_yidu_2.etymology_analysis: Auspicious compound ('Abundant Town/Capital') originating as a Western Han marquisate in 127 BCE; moved to Dongyangcheng (modern Qingzhou) in 556 CE under Northern Qi.

b_linzi.first_mention_attestation: Records of the Grand Historian (Shiji, Qi Taigong Shijia) and Bamboo Annals: Duke Xian of Qi moved the Qi capital back from Bogu to Yingqiu and renamed it Linzi (临淄) in the 9th century BCE (c. 859 BCE).
b_linzi.etymology_analysis: Locator compound meaning 'overlooking the Zi River' (地临淄水), capital of the State of Qi throughout the Eastern Zhou period.

historical_names.name: Yingqiu
historical_names.source: Records of the Grand Historian (Shiji): Jiang Ziya (Taigong Wang) was enfeoffed at Yingqiu (营丘) at the founding of the Western Zhou dynasty.
historical_names.notes: Ancient capital of the State of Qi (modern Linzi District, Zibo, Shandong).

b_shouguang.first_mention_attestation: Book of Han (Hanshu, juan 28): Shouguang County (寿光县) was established in the Western Han dynasty under Beihai Commandery.
b_shouguang.etymology_analysis: Auspicious Western Han county name ('Longevity and Radiance'), traditionally linked to a Warring States petition for longevity presented by local elders to the King of Qi.

b_linqu.first_mention_attestation: Book of Han (Hanshu, juan 28) and Yuanhe Junxian Tuzhi (juan 10): Linqu County (临朐县) was established in the Western Han dynasty under Qi Commandery.
b_linqu.etymology_analysis: Locator compound meaning 'overlooking Mount Qu' (东有朐山，因以为名), attested from the Western Han dynasty.

historical_names.name: Pianyi
historical_names.source: Linqu County historical records and Analects / Zuo Zhuan traditions: Western Zhou and Spring and Autumn fief of Pianyi (骈邑).
historical_names.notes: Modern Linqu County, Weifang, Shandong.

historical_names.name: Quyi
historical_names.source: Linqu County historical records and Analects / Zuo Zhuan traditions: Western Zhou and Spring and Autumn fief of Pianyi (骈邑).
historical_names.notes: Modern Linqu County, Weifang, Shandong.

b_beihai.first_mention_attestation: Book of Han (Hanshu, juan 28): Beihai Commandery (北海郡) was established during the reign of Emperor Jing of Han (157–141 BCE, c. 148 BCE); Sui later renamed Xiami County to Beihai County in 606 CE.
b_beihai.etymology_analysis: Directional compound ('North Sea'), referring to the commandery's position bordering the Bohai / Laizhou Bay in northern Shandong.

b_changyi.first_mention_attestation: History of Song (Songshi) and Changyi historical records: in 962 CE (Jianlong 3 of Northern Song), Beihai Commandery (北海军) was established and Changyi County (昌邑县) was created at modern Changyi, Shandong.
b_changyi.etymology_analysis: Auspicious compound ('Prosperous Town'). Founded in 962 CE under the Northern Song dynasty, post-dating the 867 CE baseline (distinct from the Han-era Changyi in southwestern Shandong).

historical_names.name: Duchang
historical_names.source: Changyi historical records and Old Book of Tang (juan 38): Qin dynasty established Duchang County (都昌县) in 221 BCE, abolished in Tang (623 CE).
historical_names.notes: Modern Changyi, Weifang, Shandong.

b_zichuan.first_mention_attestation: Book of Sui (Suishu, juan 30) and Old Book of Tang (juan 38): in 598 CE (Kaihuang 18 of Sui), Beiqiu County was renamed Zichuan County (淄川县) at modern Zichuan, Zibo.
b_zichuan.etymology_analysis: Named after the Zi River (淄水) in central Shandong. Note that the Western Han Zichuan Kingdom (菑川国, 164 BCE) was centered further east at Ju County, whereas Zichuan County at this site dates to 598 CE.

historical_names.name: Banyang
historical_names.source: Taiping Huanyu Ji (juan 19) and Book of Sui (juan 30): Western Han Banyang County (般阳县), renamed Beiqiu (贝丘) in 428 CE (Liu Song).
historical_names.notes: Modern Zichuan District, Zibo, Shandong.

historical_names.name: Beiqiu
historical_names.source: Taiping Huanyu Ji (juan 19) and Book of Sui (juan 30): Western Han Banyang County (般阳县), renamed Beiqiu (贝丘) in 428 CE (Liu Song).
historical_names.notes: Modern Zichuan District, Zibo, Shandong.

b_zouping.first_mention_attestation: Book of Han (Hanshu, juan 28) and Old Book of Tang (juan 38): Zouping County (邹平县) was established in the Western Han dynasty under Jinan Commandery.
b_zouping.etymology_analysis: Western Han county name combining 'Zou' (related to neighboring Liangzou 梁邹) and 'ping' (level plain). Temporarily named Pingyuan under Northern Qi before Sui restored Zouping.

b_changshan.first_mention_attestation: Book of Sui (Suishu, juan 30) and Yuanhe Junxian Tuzhi (juan 11): in 598 CE (Kaihuang 18 of Sui), Wuqiang County was renamed Changshan County (长山县).
b_changshan.etymology_analysis: Named in 598 CE after the elongated mountain range (Changbai Mountain 长白山) in its territory; succeeded Han Yuling and Northern Dynasties Wuqiang.

historical_names.name: Yuling
historical_names.source: Book of Han (juan 28) and Yuanhe Junxian Tuzhi: Western Han Yuling County (于陵县), renamed Wuqiang (武强) in the Northern Dynasties.
historical_names.notes: Merged into Zouping County in 1955.

historical_names.name: Wuqiang
historical_names.source: Book of Han (juan 28) and Yuanhe Junxian Tuzhi: Western Han Yuling County (于陵县), renamed Wuqiang (武强) in the Northern Dynasties.
historical_names.notes: Merged into Zouping County in 1955.

b_anxi.first_mention_attestation: Book of the Later Han (Hou Hanshu) and Old Book of Tang (juan 39): during the Yuanhe era (84–87 CE) of Emperor Zhang of Han, Anxian County was renamed Anxi (安熹/安喜); Northern Qi also renamed Lunu to Anxi, and Tang restored Anxi in 621 CE as the seat of Dingzhou.
b_anxi.etymology_analysis: Auspicious Eastern Han renaming of Anxian ('Pacified Danger') to Anxi ('Peace and Joy', 安熹/安喜); served as the prefectural seat of Dingzhou in the Tang dynasty.

historical_names.name: Lunu
historical_names.source: Book of Han (juan 28) and Old Book of Tang (juan 39): Western Han Lunu County (154 BCE) and Anxian Marquisate (124 BCE) in Zhongshan.
historical_names.notes: Modern Dingzhou, Hebei.

historical_names.name: Anxian
historical_names.source: Book of Han (juan 28) and Old Book of Tang (juan 39): Western Han Lunu County (154 BCE) and Anxian Marquisate (124 BCE) in Zhongshan.
historical_names.notes: Modern Dingzhou, Hebei.

b_wangdu.first_mention_attestation: Established as Wangdu County (望都县) under Zhongshan Commandery in 201 BCE (6th year of Han Gaozu), as recorded in the Book of Han (Han Shu, Geography Treatise).
b_wangdu.etymology_analysis: Named after Mount Wangdu (望都山), south of Mount Yao; Han commentary by Zhang Yan notes that Emperor Yao's mother Qingdu ascended Mount Yao to gaze toward Mount Wangdu, giving the county its name. Renamed Qingdu in 1173 CE under the Jin Dynasty and restored to Wangdu in 1749 CE.

b_yi.first_mention_attestation: Established as Yi County (易县) in 597 CE (Sui Kaihuang 17) as the seat of Yizhou (易州), as recorded in the Book of Sui (Sui Shu, Geography Treatise).
b_yi.etymology_analysis: Named after the Yi River (易水), which flows through the county; the Sui Dynasty established Yi County in 597 CE on the former site of Gu'an County as the administrative seat of Yizhou.

historical_names.name: Gu'an
historical_names.source: Book of Han (Han Shu, Geography Treatise, 2 CE)
historical_names.notes: Western Han established Gu'an County (故安县) under Zhuo Commandery, renamed Gu'an (固安县) in Western Jin before Sui founded Yi County on the site in 597 CE.

historical_names.name: Gu'an
historical_names.source: Book of Han (Han Shu, Geography Treatise, 2 CE)
historical_names.notes: Western Han established Gu'an County (故安县) under Zhuo Commandery, renamed Gu'an (固安县) in Western Jin before Sui founded Yi County on the site in 597 CE.

b_rongcheng.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Rongcheng County (容城县) under Zhuo Commandery in the Book of Han (Han Shu, Geography Treatise, 2 CE); the modern site was renamed Rongcheng County in 742 CE under Tang Yizhou.
b_rongcheng.etymology_analysis: Attested in Western Han under Zhuo Commandery; local gazetteers associate the name with the Han enfeoffment of the You Rong (有容) lineage. On the modern site, Han Fanyang / Sui Qiu County was renamed Quanzhong in 697 CE and Rongcheng in 742 CE.

b_laishui.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Laishui County (涞水县) under Shanggu Commandery in the Book of Sui (Sui Shu, Geography Treatise, completed 636 CE), following the Sui Dynasty renaming of Qiu County.
b_laishui.etymology_analysis: Named after the Lai River (涞水, historical name of the Juma River) flowing through the area; the Sui Dynasty renamed the Han-era Qiu County (遒县) to Laishui County.

historical_names.name: Qiu
historical_names.source: Book of Han (Han Shu, Geography Treatise, 2 CE)
historical_names.notes: Western Han established Qiu County (遒县) under Zhuo Commandery, which retained that name until the Sui Dynasty.

b_hejian.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Hejian Principality/Commandery (河间国/河间郡) in Western Han (abolished/divided in 165 BCE, 15th year of Emperor Wen), recorded in Shiji and Book of Han (Han Shu); Sui Dynasty renamed Wuyuan County to Hejian County.

morphemes.translation: river (the Nine Rivers / Yellow River channels)

b_hejian.etymology_analysis: A locator compound meaning 'between the rivers,' referring to the lowland region between the ancient Nine Rivers (九河) channels of the lower Yellow River as described in the Yu Gong and Shui Jing Zhu.

b_leshou.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Leshou County (乐寿县) in early Renshou era (c. 601 CE) under the Sui Dynasty to avoid the naming taboo of Yang Guang (Emperor Yang of Sui), recorded in the Book of Sui (Sui Shu).
b_leshou.etymology_analysis: An auspicious compound meaning 'joy and longevity,' adopted in 601 CE when Sui Renshou replaced Guangcheng (广城) due to the imperial naming taboo on the character 广 (Guang).

historical_names.name: Lecheng
historical_names.source: Book of Han (Han Shu, Geography Treatise, 2 CE)
historical_names.notes: Western Han established Lecheng County (乐成县), which Sui renamed Guangcheng County in 598 CE before changing it to Leshou in 601 CE.

historical_names.name: Guangcheng
historical_names.source: Book of Han (Han Shu, Geography Treatise, 2 CE)
historical_names.notes: Western Han established Lecheng County (乐成县), which Sui renamed Guangcheng County in 598 CE before changing it to Leshou in 601 CE.

b_shucheng.first_mention_attestation: Established as Shucheng County (束城县) in 596 CE (Sui Kaihuang 16) under Yingzhou, recorded in the Book of Sui (Sui Shu, Geography Treatise) and Tang Yingzhou records.
b_shucheng.etymology_analysis: Established in 596 CE under the Sui Dynasty in the Hejian region, continuing as a county under Tang Yingzhou until its merger in 1073 CE.

b_mo.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Mo County (莫县) and Mozhou (莫州) from Mao (鄚) in 725 CE (Tang Kaiyuan 13), as recorded in the Old Book of Tang and New Book of Tang.

morphemes.translation: Mo (simplified form of ancient toponym Mao 鄚)

b_mo.etymology_analysis: In 725 CE, Emperor Xuanzong of Tang simplified the placename character 鄚 (Mao) to 莫 (Mo) for both the prefecture (Mozhou) and its seat (Mo County).

historical_names.name: Mao
historical_names.source: Book of Han (Han Shu, Geography Treatise, 2 CE)
historical_names.notes: Western Han established Mao County (鄚县) under Zhuo Commandery, which served as the seat of Tang Maozhou (鄚州) from 711 CE until the 725 CE orthographic change.

b_wenan.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Wen'an County (文安县) under Bohai Commandery in the Book of Han (Han Shu, Geography Treatise, 2 CE).
b_wenan.etymology_analysis: An auspicious administrative name meaning 'civil order and peace,' established in the Western Han Dynasty under Bohai Commandery.

b_qingyuan.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Qingyuan County (清苑县) in 598 CE (Sui Kaihuang 18) from Yingzhou's Yongning County (and earlier established briefly in Northern Wei under Gaoyang Commandery), recorded in the Book of Sui (Sui Shu).
b_qingyuan.etymology_analysis: First created by Northern Wei and permanently restored in 598 CE when Sui Kaihuang renamed Yongning County to Qingyuan to avoid duplication with Gaozhou's Yongning County.

historical_names.name: Lexiang
historical_names.source: Book of Han (Han Shu, Geography Treatise, 2 CE)
